items.stem: Which sequence of events accurately reflects the passage’s progression from the July intervention to the researchers’ qualified conclusion?
choices: The team opened the rafts; algae fell in August; the comparison canal showed a smaller decline; heavy rain caused a spike; the raft-covered canal recovered sooner; the team concluded that shade alone was sufficient.

The team opened the rafts; algae fell in August; the city reduced fertilizer runoff; heavy rain caused a spike; the raft-covered canal recovered sooner; the team concluded that the rafts had no measurable benefit.
The team opened the rafts; heavy rain caused an algae spike; algae then fell in August; the comparison canal showed a smaller decline; the team concluded that runoff reduction explained the recovery.

The team opened the rafts; algae fell in August while runoff was also reduced; the comparison canal showed a smaller decline; heavy rain caused a spike; the raft-covered canal returned to its previous levels sooner; the researchers concluded that the rafts’ benefit depended on water movement and nutrient control.
items.stimulus: In May, a research team installed floating plant rafts in one of two city canals, expecting the rafts’ shade to reduce algae growth. The first samples instead showed more algae beneath the rafts than in the uncovered water. The team attributed this surprise not to a failure of shading but to the rafts’ blocking the wind, which left nutrient-rich water near the surface. In July, they cut openings in the rafts to allow more mixing. Algae levels fell in August, but the city had also reduced fertilizer runoff that month, so the researchers could not assign the decline entirely to the rafts. A nearby canal without rafts received the same runoff reduction and showed a smaller decline. After a later heavy rain washed nutrients into both canals, algae briefly spiked in each, yet the raft-covered canal returned to its previous levels sooner. The researchers concluded that the rafts’ benefit depended on restoring water movement and limiting nutrient accumulation, rather than on shade alone.
items.explanation: Choice D preserves the later sequence: “In July, they cut openings in the rafts to allow more mixing”; “Algae levels fell in August” while fertilizer runoff was also reduced; the nearby canal showed “a smaller decline”; “a later heavy rain” caused a spike; the raft-covered canal “returned to its previous levels sooner”; and the researchers concluded that the benefit depended on “restoring water movement and limiting nutrient accumulation.”

per_choice.correct: Choice D preserves the later sequence: “In July, they cut openings in the rafts to allow more mixing”; “Algae levels fell in August” while fertilizer runoff was also reduced; the nearby canal showed “a smaller decline”; “a later heavy rain” caused a spike; the raft-covered canal “returned to its previous levels sooner”; and the researchers concluded that the benefit depended on “restoring water movement and limiting nutrient accumulation.”
per_choice.trap: Choice A is attractive because it includes the major later events, but it changes the qualified conclusion into the claim that “shade alone was sufficient.” Choice C reverses the August decline and the later rain-related spike, while Choice B incorrectly turns the evidence into a conclusion that the rafts had no benefit.

items.trap: Choice A is attractive because it includes the major later events, but it changes the qualified conclusion into the claim that “shade alone was sufficient.” Choice C reverses the August decline and the later rain-related spike, while Choice B incorrectly turns the evidence into a conclusion that the rafts had no benefit.
items.tests: Order of events and what the passage says caused what.

items.stem: Which choice best paraphrases the point made in the sentence “To address this problem, archivists attached explanations to uncertain terms rather than silently replacing them with modern equivalents”?
choices: The archivists preserved questionable expressions and explained them instead of secretly changing them into contemporary language.
The archivists replaced unfamiliar expressions with modern terms so that every search would produce more matches.
The archivists removed uncertain words from the diaries because explanations would make the records less readable.
The archivists used modern equivalents only when they could prove that the original crew expressions had been inaccurate.
items.stimulus: When the Harbor Museum began digitizing its collection of sailors' diaries, staff expected the work to make the records easier to search without changing what they meant. Yet many entries used tide names, nicknames, and abbreviations that only made sense within particular crews, so a searchable transcript could be more legible than the original while being less informative. To address this problem, archivists attached explanations to uncertain terms rather than silently replacing them with modern equivalents. They also preserved crossings-out and awkward grammar, because those features sometimes revealed whether a sentence had been written during an event or reconstructed later. This caution slowed the project: users had to consult notes, and some searches returned fewer apparent matches than a simplified transcript would have. The loss was partly offset by a discovery: clusters of repeated nicknames and tide expressions allowed researchers to link diaries whose authors had never identified one another. Thus, the archive's usefulness came not from removing ambiguity but from making the locations and limits of ambiguity visible. Digitization, in this case, did not turn messy testimony into neutral data; it gave readers a more accountable way to encounter its messiness.
items.explanation: Choice A preserves both parts of the sentence: the archivists added explanations for uncertain terms and did not silently substitute modern equivalents. The passage says they “attached explanations” and avoided “silently replacing” the expressions.

per_choice.correct: Choice A preserves both parts of the sentence: the archivists added explanations for uncertain terms and did not silently substitute modern equivalents. The passage says they “attached explanations” and avoided “silently replacing” the expressions.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is attractive because the passage discusses searchability, but it reverses the archivists’ decision to preserve the original terms. Choices C and D add removals or proof requirements that the sentence does not state.

items.trap: Choice B is attractive because the passage discusses searchability, but it reverses the archivists’ decision to preserve the original terms. Choices C and D add removals or proof requirements that the sentence does not state.
items.tests: Restating a stretch of text without adding or losing meaning.

items.stem:
At first glance, this finding might seem to turn the tool library into a social institution rather than a lending service. Yet that contrast is too neat. In one library, attendance rose after the inventory shrank, because members came to advise newcomers and share workarounds; still, when a broken drill delayed a renovation, borrowers complained.

The tension matters because it shows that practical and social functions need not compete. Rather than replacing utility with sociability, the library’s design lets each reinforce the other: borrowing gives strangers a reason to meet, and meetings reveal skills that make borrowing more effective. Thus, a survey that counts only loans will not necessarily be wrong, but it will be incomplete. The library succeeds not when social contact substitutes for access, but when contact makes access more usable.

Which choice best describes the function of the second paragraph, beginning with “At first glance, this finding might seem to turn the tool library into a social institution rather than a lending service”?
choices: It abandons the practical measure introduced earlier and argues that attendance is the only valid measure of success.
It presents an apparent opposition between the library’s social and practical roles, then uses a specific case to show why that opposition is too simple.
It explains that a smaller inventory always increases attendance and proves that borrowing is no longer important.
It summarizes the final conclusion that social contact makes access more usable without presenting any complicating evidence.
items.stimulus: Researchers assessing neighborhood tool libraries often begin with a practical metric: how many drills, ladders, and saws circulate each month. This measure makes sense because a library that rarely lends anything may be serving little practical purpose. But interviews with members reveal a less visible function: the library gives neighbors a reason to exchange advice, recommend adaptations, and recognize one another’s skills.
items.explanation: The paragraph first raises the apparent contrast between “a social institution” and “a lending service.” It then complicates that contrast with the library where attendance rose after the inventory shrank but borrowers still complained when “a broken drill delayed a renovation.”

per_choice.correct: The paragraph first raises the apparent contrast between “a social institution” and “a lending service.” It then complicates that contrast with the library where attendance rose after the inventory shrank but borrowers still complained when “a broken drill delayed a renovation.”
per_choice.trap: Choice D is attractive because it states an idea developed later in the passage, but the second paragraph does not give the final synthesis. Choice C treats one unusual result as a general rule, and Choice A incorrectly says the practical measure is abandoned.

items.trap: Choice D is attractive because it states an idea developed later in the passage, but the second paragraph does not give the final synthesis. Choice C treats one unusual result as a general rule, and Choice A incorrectly says the practical measure is abandoned.
items.tests: How the passage is organised and what a part contributes to the whole.

items.stem: As used in the passage, “a reserve” most nearly means:
choices: A deliberately restrained or unfilled visual area whose quietness gives greater emphasis to other features
A supply of building materials held back for possible use on the north wall
A financial fund set aside to pay for later changes to the library
An unfinished surface that Sato intended to decorate once the drawings were complete
items.stimulus: When architect Niko Sato reopened his sketches for the Riverside Library, he found that the earliest pages looked careless only because they recorded decisions before he had learned to explain them. At first glance, the drawings seemed to favor decoration: colored tiles, carved vents, and a staircase that curved like a ribbon. In one margin, however, Sato wrote “economy,” meaning not an effort to make construction inexpensive but a disciplined refusal to spend visual attention everywhere at once. He called the unadorned north wall “a reserve,” not because materials had been set aside for it, but because its restraint allowed the entrance to feel more animated. Sato also tempered the bright tiles with broad areas of plaster, so that the colors would register as accents rather than as a continuous spectacle. When the committee asked him to cover the north wall with a mural, he did not yield to their fear that an undecorated surface would seem unfinished. Instead, he altered the lighting near the wall, giving its quietness a purpose that the original drawings had only implied. Years later, visitors often praised the library’s richness, though much of that richness depended on what Sato had chosen not to add.
items.explanation: Choice A fits the passage’s explanation that the north wall’s restraint allowed “the entrance to feel more animated.” The wall functions as a purposeful area of visual quiet, not as stored material or an unfinished design.

per_choice.correct: Choice A fits the passage’s explanation that the north wall’s restraint allowed “the entrance to feel more animated.” The wall functions as a purposeful area of visual quiet, not as stored material or an unfinished design.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is attractive because “reserve” can mean something set aside, but the passage explicitly says the term does not refer to materials being held back. Choice D mistakes intentional restraint for incompletion, while Choice C applies an unsupported financial meaning.

items.trap: Choice B is attractive because “reserve” can mean something set aside, but the passage explicitly says the term does not refer to materials being held back. Choice D mistakes intentional restraint for incompletion, while Choice C applies an unsupported financial meaning.
items.tests: The meaning a word carries here, which is often not its most common one.

items.stem:
Engineer Sol Kwan argued that brightness was the primary cause of disruption and predicted that dimming either color would reduce the problem in roughly the same way. To test the competing claims, researchers installed adjustable fixtures at six previously unlit stretches and alternated their color and intensity each night. At high intensity, amber fixtures attracted 19 percent fewer moths than white fixtures, but at low intensity the two colors produced no significant difference in visits. Velez therefore narrowed her claim: color appeared to matter when light was bright enough to disrupt moths, not independently of intensity.

A six-month follow-up measured egg clusters rather than visits and found 11 percent more clusters near high-intensity amber fixtures than near high-intensity white ones; the two low-intensity conditions again did not differ. Because reed density could still influence egg-laying, researchers compared only stretches whose reed density changed similarly during the study. Amber still produced 7 percent more egg clusters in that comparison, but it involved only four stretches. The report consequently described amber lighting as a promising supplement to dimming, not a substitute for it: the color effect was conditional, and the evidence for a lasting reproductive benefit remained provisional.

Which result from the adjustable-lamp trial most directly supports Velez’s narrowed claim that color matters when light is bright enough to disrupt moths, but not independently of intensity?
choices: At high intensity, amber fixtures attracted 19 percent fewer moths than white fixtures, while at low intensity the two colors produced no significant difference in visits.
In the initial survey, matched amber fixtures received 22 percent more moth visits than white fixtures.
At low intensity, amber and white fixtures produced no significant difference in visits.
At high intensity, amber fixtures attracted moths, whereas the low-intensity fixtures were installed at previously unlit stretches.
items.stimulus: Larkhaven replaced forty canal lamps with amber LEDs after residents complained that white light seemed to empty the paths of moths. Ecologist Mara Velez claimed that light color, rather than brightness alone, determines how severely lamps disrupt moth activity. In an initial survey, matched amber fixtures received 22 percent more moth visits than white fixtures. However, the canal stretches with amber fixtures also contained 31 percent more reeds, and the survey counted visits rather than egg-laying.
items.explanation: Choice A supplies both parts of the narrowed claim: when intensity was high, changing color produced a difference, but when intensity was low, the colors did not differ significantly. The trial therefore shows a conditional color effect rather than an effect independent of brightness.

per_choice.correct: Choice A supplies both parts of the narrowed claim: when intensity was high, changing color produced a difference, but when intensity was low, the colors did not differ significantly. The trial therefore shows a conditional color effect rather than an effect independent of brightness.
per_choice.trap: Choice C is attractive because it supports the claim’s low-intensity limitation, but by itself it does not show that color matters at high intensity. Choice B comes from the confounded initial survey, and Choice D does not report a meaningful comparison between color conditions.

items.trap: Choice C is attractive because it supports the claim’s low-intensity limitation, but by itself it does not show that color matters at high intensity. Choice B comes from the confounded initial survey, and Choice D does not report a meaningful comparison between color conditions.
items.tests: Identifying a claim and what would strengthen or weaken it.

items.stem:
A case devoted to the 1978 steel strike includes a dented lunch pail, a photograph of locked gates, and three sentences about "community resilience." It omits the workers' petition, whose handwritten pages are stored in the museum archive, because, the curator told me, the petition "complicated the visual story." Yet the omission is conspicuous: the photograph's caption praises cooperation while the empty space beside it seems to ask what cooperation cost. I found myself less interested in correcting the exhibit than in watching it teach visitors how to look.

Children hurried toward a video of robotic arms, while an older woman lingered before the lunch pail and read its label twice. The museum had intended to make progress feel inevitable, but these pauses restored a little uncertainty to the past. That uncertainty did not weaken the museum's story; it made the story finally belong to people rather than to the banner.

The sentence “I found myself less interested in correcting the exhibit than in watching it teach visitors how to look” primarily serves to
choices: identify the workers’ petition as the narrator’s main evidence that the exhibit is factually false
show that the narrator has stopped caring whether the museum’s historical claims are accurate
shift the narrator’s attention from correcting the exhibit’s omissions to observing how the exhibit shapes visitors’ interpretation
explain why the museum’s display of the lunch pail is more reliable than its written captions
items.stimulus: On Saturday mornings, visitors to the Eastmere Museum of Industry pass beneath a banner reading WE BUILT TOMORROW. Inside, polished displays trace the town's rise from foundries to software firms, and a recorded voice describes each transition as if it had been planned from the beginning. The exhibit is not false, exactly, but its confidence makes accident look like intention.
items.explanation: The sentence shifts the narrator’s focus from “correcting the exhibit” to observing how it “teach[es] visitors how to look.” It prepares for the next paragraph, which describes how different visitors respond to the displays.

per_choice.correct: The sentence shifts the narrator’s focus from “correcting the exhibit” to observing how it “teach[es] visitors how to look.” It prepares for the next paragraph, which describes how different visitors respond to the displays.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is attractive because the narrator expresses reduced interest in correction, but the sentence does not say accuracy no longer matters. Choice A focuses on the petition introduced earlier, and Choice D invents a comparison between the artifact and the captions.

items.trap: Choice B is attractive because the narrator expresses reduced interest in correction, but the sentence does not say accuracy no longer matters. Choice A focuses on the petition introduced earlier, and Choice D invents a comparison between the artifact and the captions.
items.tests: Why a sentence or paragraph is there, and the author's attitude.

items.stem:
Dorian laughed at the card and told her to throw out the repair ledgers, since “nobody wants a list of people who never came back.” Ren said she would, then spent her lunch reading the margins, where Vale had noted which customers could not afford a new spring and which preferred a repair to a replacement. In the basement, she found a tall clock stopped at 4:17, its face removed and its pendulum hanging from a nail. She tried the brass key in twelve locks before noticing that the clock's winding hole had been drilled slightly off-center, as if someone had once tried to make it usable for a different key.

On Friday, Dorian offered Ren the clock because, he said, she was the only person who had treated it as more than scrap; she refused the gift but asked permission to keep working after the auction. He agreed, mostly because he wanted the shop cleared, and watched as she sorted Vale's notes into envelopes addressed to the customers whose repairs were still waiting. Ren did not repair the tall clock that night; instead, she placed its loose pendulum beside the envelopes and wrote on the door, “Please knock before deciding what is broken.” At dawn, she found Dorian reading the note, holding the brass key in his palm, while the three crates remained open behind him.

Dorian's changing treatment of the clock and the ledgers most strongly characterizes him as someone who
choices: initially values efficiency but becomes willing to reconsider what he had dismissed
believes that Mr. Vale's customers should be protected from the auction
is eager to preserve every object connected with his father's work
understands from the beginning why Ren separates the clocks from the crates
items.stimulus: When Ren was hired to empty Mr. Vale's clock-repair shop, Dorian, his son, warned her that the work had to be finished before Saturday's auction. Ren brought three crates marked SELL, GIVE, and THINK, though the last was only a wooden fruit box with a question mark penciled on its side. She moved quickly through the front room, but whenever a clock had been opened and left with its screws in a saucer, she closed the crate in her hands and set that clock apart. Beneath a drawer she found a brass key taped to a card that read, in Vale's cramped hand, “For the day the clock stops.”
items.explanation: Dorian first laughs at the card and tells Ren to discard the ledgers, but later offers her the clock and is found “reading the note, holding the brass key in his palm.” These details suggest that his practical, dismissive attitude may be changing. The passage does not show that he prioritizes protecting customers, preserves every object, or understands Ren's purpose from the beginning.

per_choice.correct: Dorian first laughs at the card and tells Ren to discard the ledgers, but later offers her the clock and is found “reading the note, holding the brass key in his palm.” These details suggest that his practical, dismissive attitude may be changing. The passage does not show that he prioritizes protecting customers, preserves every object, or understands Ren's purpose from the beginning.
per_choice.trap: Choice C is attractive because Dorian offers Ren the clock and later holds the brass key, but the passage shows that he initially treats the shop's objects as things to clear rather than things to preserve.

items.trap: Choice C is attractive because Dorian offers Ren the clock and later holds the brass key, but the passage shows that he initially treats the shop's objects as things to clear rather than things to preserve.
items.tests: What a literary passage shows about a person through action and detail.

items.stem:
Passage 2
Historian and harbor organizer Julian Ortiz agrees that old seawalls should not automatically survive, but he objects to treating residents as visitors. Working piers, ferry landings, and fishing paths may seem ecologically untidy, yet they encode skills and obligations that no habitat survey records. For Ortiz, a resilient marsh includes a public able to recognize its changes and claim a role in maintaining it; access is not a compromise but a condition of resilience. He therefore favors modular infrastructure that can be moved as channels shift, along with paid stewardship programs linking ecological monitoring to local livelihoods. He is skeptical of Sen’s “temporary” ideal: structures can be physically removable yet politically permanent if communities build identities around them.

The primary difference between Sen's and Ortiz's approaches is that they assign different importance to
choices: whether infrastructure can be removed physically without ending its political significance
whether ecological monitoring should influence changes to restoration projects
whether old seawalls should be allowed to remain in a changing marsh
whether a resilient marsh should support varied species as well as withstand storms
items.stimulus:
Passage 1
Coastal ecologist Mira Sen argues that marsh restoration should begin by removing obsolete embankments and allowing tidal channels to re-form. Her criterion is not resemblance to a historical map but the capacity to absorb storms and support varied species. She concedes that towns need access, but calls boardwalks and viewing platforms “careful compromises,” valuable mainly when they direct visitors away from recovering zones. Sen warns that designing habitat around current recreational habits can freeze a damaged shoreline into an attractive exhibit. Monitoring should therefore guide temporary interventions, with managers willing to undo even successful-looking structures if marsh processes improve without them.
items.explanation: Sen favors temporary interventions that managers can undo when marsh processes improve, while Ortiz warns that structures can be physically removable yet politically permanent because communities may build identities around them. Both writers value monitoring, reject automatically preserving old seawalls, and connect resilience with ecological function.

per_choice.correct: Sen favors temporary interventions that managers can undo when marsh processes improve, while Ortiz warns that structures can be physically removable yet politically permanent because communities may build identities around them. Both writers value monitoring, reject automatically preserving old seawalls, and connect resilience with ecological function.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is attractive because both writers discuss monitoring and changing interventions, but that is an area of agreement rather than their primary difference.

items.trap: Choice B is attractive because both writers discuss monitoring and changing interventions, but that is an area of agreement rather than their primary difference.
items.tests: Where two passages agree, differ, or would answer each other.

items.stem:
Merchant charts rendered the marsh as a set of geometric blocks, with property boundaries receiving sharper lines than waterways. They omitted narrow channels that pilots used when larger routes became impassable. At first, this omission seemed like a simplification caused by the limits of printing. But pilots' notes repeatedly named those channels and marked their depth, even when the printed charts left the corresponding spaces blank. The omitted features were therefore not unknown; they were inconvenient to a chart designed to make ownership legible.

Bell calls these charts administrative portraits: their apparent neatness records a governing purpose as much as a shoreline. When a later harbor authority combined the two traditions, it retained the block outlines from the merchants' charts but copied the channels from the pilots' notes. The hybrid map was more useful to navigators, yet its official format preserved the visual hierarchy that made property seem more permanent than water. Bell concludes that maps should be read as arguments about what matters in a landscape, not as neutral mirrors of what is there.

Which sentence best supports the claim that merchant charts emphasized property ownership more strongly than the practical needs of navigators?
choices: Merchant charts rendered the marsh as a set of geometric blocks, with property boundaries receiving sharper lines than waterways.
They omitted narrow channels that pilots used when larger routes became impassable.
But pilots' notes repeatedly named those channels and marked their depth, even when the printed charts left the corresponding spaces blank.
When a later harbor authority combined the two traditions, it retained the block outlines from the merchants' charts but copied the channels from the pilots' notes.
items.stimulus: For much of the nineteenth century, maps of the Bellwater Harbor marsh circulated as both navigational aids and records of commercial control. In a recent study, cartographer Imani Bell compared printed charts commissioned by merchants with handwritten route notes kept by local pilots. She compared not only the features each document included but also the kinds of decisions each document enabled. Bell's question was not which map was accurate but why the same shoreline looked different in each kind of record.
items.explanation: The sentence states that merchant charts gave sharper lines to property boundaries than to waterways, directly supporting the claim that ownership received greater visual emphasis than navigation. The other choices show omitted channels, the pilots' knowledge of them, or the later hybrid map, but they do not state the merchant charts' hierarchy as directly.

per_choice.correct: The sentence states that merchant charts gave sharper lines to property boundaries than to waterways, directly supporting the claim that ownership received greater visual emphasis than navigation. The other choices show omitted channels, the pilots' knowledge of them, or the later hybrid map, but they do not state the merchant charts' hierarchy as directly.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is attractive because the omitted channels show that the charts were less useful to navigators, but it does not by itself identify the stronger emphasis on property ownership.

items.trap: Choice B is attractive because the omitted channels show that the charts were less useful to navigators, but it does not by itself identify the stronger emphasis on property ownership.
items.tests: Which sentence best supports a claim - the question shape the digital SAT leans on hardest.

items.stem:
Museum records indicate that the artist, Marisol Chen, bought gray pigment in 1934, though the surviving invoices list no blue pigment. A letter does record that city officials objected to the mural's labor scenes, so the curator initially attributed the altered sky and missing boats to censorship. That explanation became less secure when scraping at two edge panels found the same pale layer beneath later varnish, in places where officials would have had little reason to intervene. Lina noted that the evidence could show a sequence of changes without showing why Chen made them.

At a workshop, visitors compared the visible mural with the infrared image. Many interpreted the covered boats as proof that Chen had abandoned realism, while Lina argued that an underdrawing records possibilities, not necessarily a settled intention. She proposed labeling the mural as “revised during painting” rather than “censored.” The wording frustrated visitors who wanted a decisive story, but it preserved a distinction between what the material evidence establishes and what the archive merely suggests.

Which conclusion about the boats beneath the mural's visible paint is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: Their presence shows that Chen considered including boats, but it does not establish that she intended them to remain in the finished mural.
Their removal proves that city officials censored the mural's original design.
Their presence demonstrates that Chen abandoned realism when she revised the mural.
Their location beneath the visible paint proves that the boats were painted before the dockworkers and cranes.
items.stimulus: At a coastal museum, conservator Lina Velez examined a 1930s mural whose dockworkers and cranes stood beneath an unusually pale sky. An archival photograph showed that the sky had once appeared darker. An infrared scan revealed boats sketched beneath the visible paint and several figures shifted from their original positions. Chemical tests found that the pale sky lay over a charcoal-gray wash, rather than over untouched plaster.
items.explanation: Lina argues that “an underdrawing records possibilities, not necessarily a settled intention.” Therefore, the covered boats show that they were considered during the painting process, but they do not prove that Chen intended them to remain in the final work. The passage specifically says the censorship explanation became less secure and does not establish the order of every painted element.

per_choice.correct: Lina argues that “an underdrawing records possibilities, not necessarily a settled intention.” Therefore, the covered boats show that they were considered during the painting process, but they do not prove that Chen intended them to remain in the final work. The passage specifically says the censorship explanation became less secure and does not establish the order of every painted element.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is attractive because the passage mentions that “city officials objected to the mural's labor scenes,” but that evidence suggests censorship without proving that officials caused the boats to be covered.

items.trap: Choice B is attractive because the passage mentions that “city officials objected to the mural's labor scenes,” but that evidence suggests censorship without proving that officials caused the boats to be covered.
items.tests: What follows from the text without being stated, staying inside what the passage supports.

items.stem:
To test that impression, the team followed three libraries through an entire growing season. They expected activity to peak at planting time and again at harvest, when people would acquire or save seeds. Instead, visits increased after seedlings failed and just before neighborhood festivals, when gardeners sought advice about unfamiliar conditions. A packet often mattered less than the conversation surrounding it: experienced gardeners translated a label into practical guidance about shade, soil, or watering.

These findings did not lead the researchers to dismiss conservation as incidental. The programs were most durable when their rules were flexible enough for people to exchange uncertain advice as well as accurately labeled seeds; one library's more rigid catalog reduced participation even though its records were more precise. The researchers therefore describe seed libraries as social infrastructure: they preserve biological materials by making knowledge portable and trust renewable. That description helps explain why some modest collections outlast larger programs that measure success mainly by the number of packets stored.

Which choice best states the central claim of the passage's second paragraph?
choices: Seed-library visits increased at times when gardeners needed help responding to problems or unfamiliar conditions, making conversation more important than the packet alone.
The researchers discovered that gardeners visited seed libraries most often during planting and harvest.
Experienced gardeners were responsible for explaining how shade, soil, and watering affected unfamiliar seeds.
Gardeners preferred receiving practical advice to acquiring or saving seeds at planting and harvest.
items.stimulus: In several neighborhoods, residents created seed libraries where gardeners could leave or take packets without paying. Unlike conventional seed banks, which chiefly protect genetic material under controlled conditions, these small collections operated in porches, storefronts, and community rooms. Volunteers cataloged the packets, but they also recorded stories about which varieties survived particular yards. The researchers initially treated that storytelling as a pleasant supplement to conservation, yet their observations suggested that the exchange of local knowledge was part of the library's basic function.
items.explanation: The paragraph contrasts the researchers' expectation about planting and harvest with the observed increase after seedlings failed and before festivals. It then explains that “A packet often mattered less than the conversation surrounding it,” making the first choice the paragraph's central point. The other choices state either the expectation, one supporting detail, or an overstatement of the findings.

per_choice.correct: The paragraph contrasts the researchers' expectation about planting and harvest with the observed increase after seedlings failed and before festivals. It then explains that “A packet often mattered less than the conversation surrounding it,” making the first choice the paragraph's central point. The other choices state either the expectation, one supporting detail, or an overstatement of the findings.
per_choice.trap: Choice B is attractive because planting and harvest are explicitly mentioned, but those times describe what the researchers expected, not what the study found.

items.trap: Choice B is attractive because planting and harvest are explicitly mentioned, but those times describe what the researchers expected, not what the study found.
items.tests: What the passage or a paragraph is chiefly about, as opposed to a true but minor detail.

items.stem:
From my upstairs office, I could hear visitors below but could not see their faces unless I leaned over the stairwell. On the fourth morning, a boy asked why the station map showed no route beyond the inlet, and Mara answered that the route had vanished after the 1968 storm. She did not say whether the boats had vanished, the map had vanished, or merely the town’s willingness to remember them. I assumed she was correcting a child, not the institution that had hired me.

That afternoon, while checking a drawer the museum had marked empty, I found the first director’s notebook. One entry called the bell “a signal for boats”; another called it “a ritual for those waiting,” and a final instruction told staff to omit both descriptions because “the station’s purpose should be clear.” I wanted these contradictions to settle whether Mara remembered accurately; instead, they showed me that the archive had been shaped by someone else’s wish for clarity. When Mara asked whether the bell belonged in the exhibit, I answered yes, but added, “with the uncertainty intact.” I still could not say what the bell had meant on any particular morning; I could say why the label “unverified” had been too easy.

The narrator’s decision to include the bell in the exhibit “with the uncertainty intact” most strongly characterizes the narrator as someone who
choices: has abandoned all confidence in the museum’s ability to preserve accurate historical evidence
has come to recognize that acknowledging ambiguity can be more accurate than imposing a definitive explanation
now believes Mara’s account is more reliable than the director’s notebook
wants visitors to decide for themselves whether the bell was used for boats or waiting families
items.stimulus: Each morning, I unlocked Harbor House, the former tide station where I had been hired to catalogue objects for a small museum. I trusted labels more than anecdotes; a label could be checked against a ledger, while a story changed slightly each time it was told. Mara, who had dispatched boats from the station for thirty years, insisted that the brass bell beside the entrance had once been rung for families waiting on the pier. I wrote “bell, purpose unverified” on my inventory sheet and moved to the next object.
items.explanation: The narrator says, “with the uncertainty intact,” after discovering contradictory records and concludes that the label “unverified” had been “too easy.” This shows a developing willingness to preserve ambiguity rather than force the evidence into a single explanation.

per_choice.correct: The narrator says, “with the uncertainty intact,” after discovering contradictory records and concludes that the label “unverified” had been “too easy.” This shows a developing willingness to preserve ambiguity rather than force the evidence into a single explanation.
per_choice.trap: Choice A overstates the narrator’s distrust of the museum, while Choice C reverses the narrator’s position by making Mara’s account definitively reliable. Choice D is plausible because the narrator leaves the issue unresolved, but the passage emphasizes accuracy in representing uncertainty rather than a desire to shift the interpretive burden to visitors.

items.trap: Choice A overstates the narrator’s distrust of the museum, while Choice C reverses the narrator’s position by making Mara’s account definitively reliable. Choice D is plausible because the narrator leaves the issue unresolved, but the passage emphasizes accuracy in representing uncertainty rather than a desire to shift the interpretive burden to visitors.
items.tests: Whose perspective is given and how it shapes what is said.

items.stem:
The team expected mild drought to improve survival, but they also considered a simpler explanation: smaller seedlings might lose water more slowly, appearing more resilient without having been physiologically primed. The nutrient-restricted seedlings were included because they could become similarly small without experiencing water shortage. Although the mild-drought group was nearly the same size as the nutrient-restricted group at the start of severe drought, its survival was substantially higher and its root-to-shoot ratio was much larger. The researchers therefore associated the survival advantage with altered allocation to roots, while cautioning that the treatment reduced final leaf area, an important measure of growth.

Compared with the seedlings that received reduced nutrients, which statement accurately describes the mild-drought group?
choices: Its survival increased by 13 percentage points, while its root-to-shoot ratio increased by 0.39.
Its survival increased by 13 percent, while its root-to-shoot ratio increased by 0.39.
Its survival increased by 13 percentage points, while its root-to-shoot ratio decreased by 0.39.
Its survival increased by 3 percentage points, while its root-to-shoot ratio increased by 0.39.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether a brief water shortage could prepare seedlings to survive a later, more severe drought. They divided otherwise identical seedlings into three groups: one received no pretreatment, one experienced mild drought, and one received reduced nutrients for the same period. After a recovery period in identical conditions, all three groups underwent seven days of severe drought. Figure 1 reports each group's height at the beginning of that drought, its survival rate afterward, its final leaf area, and its root-to-shoot mass ratio.
items.explanation: The mild-drought group had a survival rate of 74%, compared with 61% for the reduced-nutrients group, an increase of 13 percentage points. Its root-to-shoot ratio was 1.12 rather than 0.73, an increase of 0.39.

per_choice.correct: The mild-drought group had a survival rate of 74%, compared with 61% for the reduced-nutrients group, an increase of 13 percentage points. Its root-to-shoot ratio was 1.12 rather than 0.73, an increase of 0.39.
per_choice.trap: Choice B confuses a percentage-point difference with a percent difference. Choice C reverses the direction of the root-to-shoot change. Choice D uses the difference between the mild-drought group’s and the untreated group’s survival rates instead of comparing the two groups named in the question.

items.trap: Choice B confuses a percentage-point difference with a percent difference. Choice C reverses the direction of the root-to-shoot change. Choice D uses the difference between the mild-drought group’s and the untreated group’s survival rates instead of comparing the two groups named in the question.

items.stem:
Voss's result seemed to reverse Rao's explanation, but his survey also showed that first-time borrowers who attended a fifteen-minute orientation later reported slightly greater trust than first-time borrowers who did not. To test these possibilities, the research team randomly offered orientation sessions to new members at two libraries. Six months later, the offer had increased repeat borrowing but had not increased general sociability among residents who did not borrow. The contrast mattered because it separated a change in library behavior from a change in neighborhood relationships.

Taken together, the findings suggest that a tool library may function less as a trust factory than as an amplifier of trust that already exists. Rao's records capture one part of a feedback loop: borrowing may create opportunities for contact, while Voss's survey identifies trust as a condition that makes such contact more likely. The experiment indicates that a deliberate design feature can strengthen one link in that loop without automatically producing broad trust beyond the library's users.

The experiment involving orientation sessions most directly supports which conclusion about the relationship between the researchers’ findings?
choices: A designed increase in borrowing behavior does not necessarily produce broader sociability among people who do not borrow.
Repeated borrowing cannot contribute to sociability because the orientation failed to increase general trust.
Preexisting neighborhood trust is the only factor that can increase repeat borrowing.
Rao’s and Voss’s findings were both disproved once the team used random assignment.
items.stimulus: In many tool libraries, borrowing is treated as a practical service rather than a social program. Sociologist Mina Rao studied borrowing records and observations at four libraries for eighteen months, finding that members who borrowed at least four times were more likely to greet one another and exchange advice. Rao interpreted this pattern as evidence that repeated, low-stakes exchanges build familiarity, although the records could not show whether borrowing caused sociability. Economist Caleb Voss approached the same question through a survey and found that residents who already reported strong neighborhood trust were more willing to borrow unfamiliar tools, even when they had never used a library.
items.explanation: The experiment found that the orientation offer “had increased repeat borrowing but had not increased general sociability among residents who did not borrow.” This separates a change in library behavior from a broad change in neighborhood relationships and supports the passage’s description of the findings as parts of a feedback loop rather than a single automatic effect.

per_choice.correct: The experiment found that the orientation offer “had increased repeat borrowing but had not increased general sociability among residents who did not borrow.” This separates a change in library behavior from a broad change in neighborhood relationships and supports the passage’s description of the findings as parts of a feedback loop rather than a single automatic effect.
per_choice.trap: Choice B treats the failure to produce broad sociability as proof that borrowing cannot contribute to sociability, even though the passage says the experiment increased repeat borrowing. Choice C ignores the experiment’s manipulation, and Choice D falsely claims that the experiment disproved both observational findings.

items.trap: Choice B treats the failure to produce broad sociability as proof that borrowing cannot contribute to sociability, even though the passage says the experiment increased repeat borrowing. Choice C ignores the experiment’s manipulation, and Choice D falsely claims that the experiment disproved both observational findings.
items.tests: How two people, ideas or findings in the passage relate.

items.stem:
The map was commissioned to guide ships past a chain of reefs, and its maker had filled every other margin with soundings, wind arrows, and warnings. Yet where the final reef should have appeared, he drew no depth, no hazard mark, not even the customary cross. The omission mattered because the expedition that supplied the map had returned with its captain dead and its log missing three pages. Inez did not claim the blank proved a secret; she argued only that calling it accidental erased the choices visible around it.

To make her point, she compared the map with a lighthouse register from the same voyage: on the day the captain disappeared, the keeper recorded a bell ringing offshore, then crossed out the entry. A crossed-out bell, like an uncharted reef, is not a message with a single translation, but neither is it nothing. Inez leaves the map's wedge uncolored in the exhibit, resisting the easy drama of painting in a monster or the easy comfort of restoring a coastline. The empty space therefore does less to tell us what happened than to show how evidence can preserve a decision not to say.

The comparison of “A crossed-out bell” with “an uncharted reef” primarily serves to
choices: show that the lighthouse keeper and the mapmaker deliberately concealed the same specific event
suggest that both forms of evidence preserve signs of a choice while resisting a single certain interpretation
prove that the captain disappeared because the lighthouse bell warned of a reef
contrast a reliable written record with an unreliable map damaged by time
items.stimulus: In the archive's lowest drawer, beneath tax ledgers and a box of buttons, lay a map that had forgotten how to end. Its coastline stopped at a pale wedge of paper, as if the sea had taken a bite. For years, visitors treated the gap as a printer's accident; the curator, Inez Vale, called that explanation a "polite fiction." She pointed out that the map's ink grew darker around the blank, the way a voice may sharpen around a name it refuses to speak.
items.explanation: The passage states, “A crossed-out bell, like an uncharted reef, is not a message with a single translation, but neither is it nothing.” The comparison emphasizes that omissions can preserve evidence of a decision without yielding one definite meaning.

per_choice.correct: The passage states, “A crossed-out bell, like an uncharted reef, is not a message with a single translation, but neither is it nothing.” The comparison emphasizes that omissions can preserve evidence of a decision without yielding one definite meaning.
per_choice.trap: Choice A turns the analogy into proof of a shared conspiracy, which the passage does not establish. Choice C treats the bell as a confirmed warning, while Choice D wrongly presents the map as unreliable and the register as fully reliable.

items.trap: Choice A turns the analogy into proof of a shared conspiracy, which the passage does not establish. Choice C treats the bell as a confirmed warning, while Choice D wrongly presents the map as unreliable and the register as fully reliable.
items.tests: Why the author chose a particular word, image or example.

items.stem:
To determine whether seeds were absent or merely failing to emerge in the field, the ecologists collected soil cores and placed them in a greenhouse. Cores from untouched plots yielded many native seedlings, whereas cores from loosened plots yielded few. Mapping the site then showed that runoff had carried loosened soil—and the newly sown seeds within it—toward a low edge of the yard. The team installed straw barriers across the slopes and sowed the plots again.

Emergence improved after the barriers were installed, but few of the surviving plants flowered. Watching the plots, the ecologists discovered that rabbits were clipping the young plants before they could bloom. When they added wire exclosures, flowering increased sharply. The sequence showed that the restoration faced two bottlenecks in succession: seed movement first limited emergence, and rabbit browsing later limited flowering.

After the ecologists installed straw barriers and resowed the plots, which observation led them to identify the next bottleneck in the restoration?
choices: Emergence improved, but few of the surviving plants flowered.
The loosened plots yielded few seedlings in the greenhouse.
Runoff carried loosened soil toward a low edge of the yard.
The team found that untouched plots contained many native seedlings.
items.stimulus: When ecologists restored prairie on a former rail yard, they sowed native seeds after removing the remaining gravel. Although spring rainfall exceeded the forecast, few native seedlings emerged. The team initially attributed the poor emergence to compacted soil and loosened half the plots with an aerator. But after a heavy rain, the loosened plots produced fewer seedlings than untouched plots, so the team could not attribute the shortfall simply to compaction.
items.explanation: The passage says, “Emergence improved after the barriers were installed, but few of the surviving plants flowered.” This result showed that the seed-movement problem had been reduced but that another problem was preventing flowering, leading the ecologists to watch the plots and discover rabbit browsing.

per_choice.correct: The passage says, “Emergence improved after the barriers were installed, but few of the surviving plants flowered.” This result showed that the seed-movement problem had been reduced but that another problem was preventing flowering, leading the ecologists to watch the plots and discover rabbit browsing.
per_choice.trap: Choice B helped show that seeds were viable but occurred before the barriers were installed. Choice C identified the earlier seed-movement bottleneck. Choice D also contributed to the earlier diagnosis rather than prompting the investigation of the later flowering problem.

items.trap: Choice B helped show that seeds were viable but occurred before the barriers were installed. Choice C identified the earlier seed-movement bottleneck. Choice D also contributed to the earlier diagnosis rather than prompting the investigation of the later flowering problem.
items.tests: Order of events and what the passage says caused what.

items.stem:
To test whether obstruction or location explained the pattern, the team compared paired plots—one cleared and one partially obstructed—and sampled water at several downstream points. Cleared plots showed lower sediment levels near channel mouths but higher concentrations farther away, whereas obstructed plots retained more coarse material locally and released less fine sediment downstream. Because the researchers measured both the channel and downstream water, they treated “success” as reducing marsh-wide sediment redistribution, not simply making an individual channel look clean.

This definition changed the interpretation: a visually tidy channel could signal that sediment had merely been exported, while an untidy one could be holding material in place. The team cautioned that roots and reeds were not universally beneficial; after unusually high tides, dense debris could divert flow toward banks. For restoration planners, the study therefore recommends varying obstacles and monitoring where sediment goes, rather than judging a project by the speed of local clearing alone.

Which choice best paraphrases the third paragraph?
choices: The researchers recommend removing all obstructions because a clean channel is the clearest sign that restoration has succeeded.
Because debris can either retain sediment or redirect water, restoration should be evaluated by tracking sediment movement rather than by the appearance of a single channel.
The researchers conclude that roots and reeds always improve restoration because they prevent sediment from leaving the marsh under every tidal condition.
The researchers argue that unusually high tides make sediment monitoring unnecessary because dense debris will inevitably damage the banks.
items.stimulus: Researchers at Marrow Marsh expected restored channels to export accumulated sediment faster after tidal flushing because unobstructed water should move more freely. Instead, sediment accumulation declined most in plots where volunteers left tangled roots and fallen reeds in place. The result did not make flow irrelevant: strong currents removed loose material quickly, but in cleared plots they also carried fragments downstream, where those fragments broke apart and settled in slower water.
items.explanation: The paragraph explains that “a visually tidy channel could signal that sediment had merely been exported” and that “an untidy one could be holding material in place.” It then cautions that dense debris can divert flow toward banks after unusually high tides and recommends “varying obstacles and monitoring where sediment goes.” Choice B preserves these central ideas.

per_choice.correct: The paragraph explains that “a visually tidy channel could signal that sediment had merely been exported” and that “an untidy one could be holding material in place.” It then cautions that dense debris can divert flow toward banks after unusually high tides and recommends “varying obstacles and monitoring where sediment goes.” Choice B preserves these central ideas.
per_choice.trap: Choice A reverses the recommendation by treating cleanliness as the measure of success. Choice C changes the qualified benefit of roots and reeds into an absolute one. Choice D ignores the paragraph’s recommendation to monitor sediment and falsely claims that high tides eliminate the need for monitoring.

items.trap: Choice A reverses the recommendation by treating cleanliness as the measure of success. Choice C changes the qualified benefit of roots and reeds into an absolute one. Choice D ignores the paragraph’s recommendation to monitor sediment and falsely claims that high tides eliminate the need for monitoring.
items.tests: Restating a stretch of text without adding or losing meaning.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why the number of seedlings in each group was an important constant when interpreting Figure 1?
choices: The 0.0-g/L group had the control number of seedlings, so seedling number was the dependent variable.
All groups began with the same number of seedlings, so differences in mean dry mass could be attributed more specifically to nitrogen rather than to different starting populations.
The number of seedlings increased as nitrogen concentration increased, allowing the two factors to be compared.
The 5.6-g mean dry mass in Figure 1 shows that every group began with 5.6 seedlings.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seedlings for 14 days to test how nitrogen fertilizer affects growth. Each group began with seedlings of the same age and number, and the intended difference among groups was nitrogen concentration. Table 1 lists the treatment conditions, while Figure 1 shows the mean dry mass measured at the end of the experiment. The group receiving no nitrogen fertilizer provided a reference for evaluating the treated groups.
items.explanation: Table 1 indicates that every group began with the same number of seedlings. Holding starting population constant prevents unequal group size from providing an alternative explanation for differences in mean dry mass in Figure 1.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 indicates that every group began with the same number of seedlings. Holding starting population constant prevents unequal group size from providing an alternative explanation for differences in mean dry mass in Figure 1.
per_choice.trap: Choice A confuses a treatment condition with a measured variable; C incorrectly says the number varied with nitrogen; D confuses a dry-mass value with a count of seedlings.

items.trap: Choice A confuses a treatment condition with a measured variable; C incorrectly says the number varied with nitrogen; D confuses a dry-mass value with a count of seedlings.

items.stem: Which variable was measured as the response in the investigation represented by Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: Initial sucrose concentration
Mass of yeast in each flask
Carbon dioxide volume
Incubation temperature
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated whether the initial sucrose concentration affects carbon dioxide production by yeast. Each flask contained the same mass of yeast and liquid and was kept at 25°C; carbon dioxide volume was recorded during a 20-minute period. Table 1 summarizes the final measurement for each sucrose concentration, while Figure 1 shows how the measured gas volume changed during the period. The concentrations were selected to include a no-sucrose comparison and several sucrose treatments.
items.explanation: Carbon dioxide volume is recorded during the 20-minute period and summarized in Table 1 and Figure 1, so it is the measured response. Initial sucrose concentration is the manipulated variable, while yeast mass and temperature are held constant.

per_choice.correct: Carbon dioxide volume is recorded during the 20-minute period and summarized in Table 1 and Figure 1, so it is the measured response. Initial sucrose concentration is the manipulated variable, while yeast mass and temperature are held constant.
per_choice.trap: Choice A confuses the treatment with the response; choices B and D select variables that were kept constant rather than measured as outcomes.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: Why did the investigators adjust all flasks to the same initial dissolved-oxygen concentration?
choices: To make differences in oxygen change attributable to the experimental conditions rather than to different starting concentrations
To prevent oxygen exchange with the air from being mistaken for oxygen produced or consumed by the plant
To ensure that the water bath, rather than the flask, determined the temperature
To make the dark trials receive the same light intensity as the illuminated trials
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affects the net oxygen production of an aquatic plant during a 20-minute trial. Each plant flask was placed in a water bath, connected to an oxygen probe, and kept either illuminated or dark; the investigators adjusted all flasks to the same initial dissolved-oxygen concentration. After a 5-minute equilibration period, they recorded the final oxygen concentration, with the probe reading used to calculate the net change. Table 1 lists final measurements, Figure 1 summarizes net changes at each temperature, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used.
items.explanation: Using the same initial dissolved-oxygen concentration controls the starting condition, allowing the measured net changes to be compared across temperatures and light conditions. Sealing the flask, not equalizing the starting concentration, prevents oxygen exchange with air.

per_choice.correct: Using the same initial dissolved-oxygen concentration controls the starting condition, allowing the measured net changes to be compared across temperatures and light conditions. Sealing the flask, not equalizing the starting concentration, prevents oxygen exchange with air.
per_choice.trap: Choice B assigns the purpose of sealing the flask to the initial-concentration adjustment; choices C and D confuse this control with temperature control or light treatment.

items.stem: The planned 30 mg/L trial is expected to produce the same number of bubbles in 10 minutes as the 20 mg/L trial. How many more bubbles should the 30 mg/L trial produce than the 20 mg/L trial?
choices: 0 bubbles
2 bubbles
16 bubbles
160 bubbles
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how nitrate concentration affected photosynthetic oxygen production and dry mass in duckweed. Identical samples were grown under the same light intensity and temperature, and nitrate concentration was the factor varied. Table 1 gives the mean oxygen production after 10 minutes at each tested concentration, Figure 1 shows oxygen accumulation over time, and Figure 2 shows dry mass after 7 days. The researchers planned a further trial at 30 mg/L nitrate, a concentration not included in the original trials.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows that the 20 and 40 mg/L trials each produced 16 bubbles per minute. Following the local pattern, the 30 mg/L trial is predicted to produce 16 bubbles per minute as well. Thus, over 10 minutes, both trials would produce 160 bubbles, for a difference of 0 bubbles.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows that the 20 and 40 mg/L trials each produced 16 bubbles per minute. Following the local pattern, the 30 mg/L trial is predicted to produce 16 bubbles per minute as well. Thus, over 10 minutes, both trials would produce 160 bubbles, for a difference of 0 bubbles.
per_choice.trap: A student may extend the earlier upward trend and choose 2 bubbles, confuse the per-minute rate with the 10-minute total and choose 16 bubbles, or use the total without subtracting and choose 160 bubbles.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 2, what is the ratio of the gross gas volume collected at 4,000 lux to the net gas volume remaining after the background rate was removed?
items.stimulus: Researchers measured gas collected from aquatic plants exposed to different light intensities for 8 minutes. Table 1 shows the total gas volume collected at each intensity, including the 0-lux background measurement. Figure 1 shows cumulative gas collection over time for 2,000 and 8,000 lux. Figure 2 shows net gas-production rates, calculated by subtracting the 0-lux rate from each gross rate.
items.explanation: The gross volume at 4,000 lux is 11.6 mL in Table 1. Figure 2 gives a net rate of 1.30 mL per minute, which corresponds to 10.4 mL over 8 minutes. The gross-to-net ratio is 11.6 divided by 10.4, or 1.12.

items.tests: A difference, ratio, rate or average computed from displayed values.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the changes over the final catalyst-concentration interval in Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2?
choices: The reaction rate decreases at both temperatures, while the amount of substrate remaining increases.
The reaction rate continues to increase at both temperatures, but its increase is smaller than over the first interval; the amount of substrate remaining also decreases by a smaller amount.
The reaction rate increases by the same amount at both temperatures, while the substrate decreases by the same amount.
The reaction rate stops increasing at both temperatures, and the amount of substrate remaining is unchanged.
items.stimulus: Researchers measured how catalyst concentration affected the initial rate of a reaction and the amount of substrate remaining after 10 minutes. Table 1 gives rates at 25 C, while Figure 1 gives rates at 35 C across the same concentrations. Figure 2 shows the remaining substrate for those concentrations after the same 10-minute interval.
items.explanation: Table 1 and Figure 1 show that rate continues to increase at both temperatures, with a smaller gain at higher catalyst concentration. Figure 2 shows that substrate remaining continues to decrease, with a smaller decrease over the final interval.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 and Figure 1 show that rate continues to increase at both temperatures, with a smaller gain at higher catalyst concentration. Figure 2 shows that substrate remaining continues to decrease, with a smaller decrease over the final interval.
per_choice.trap: The other choices reverse one or both trends, treat the interval changes as equal, or incorrectly infer a plateau from the diminishing increase.

items.stem: According to the stated model, what distance should a damp seed released from 1.0 m travel at a wind speed of 10 m/s, even though that speed was not tested?
choices: 32 cm
35 cm
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how wind speed affects the horizontal distance traveled by dry and damp seeds released from a height of 1.0 m. A proposed model predicts that a dry seed travels D = 2 + 3v centimeters, where v is wind speed in meters per second; for a damp seed, the predicted distance is 60% of the dry-seed prediction. The model was tested at wind speeds from 2 to 8 m/s. Table 1 gives measured distances for both seed conditions, Figure 1 gives measured damp-seed distances, and Figure 2 gives the percentage of dry seeds that traveled at least 20 cm.
items.explanation: The model predicts a dry-seed distance of 2 + 3(10) = 32 cm. The damp-seed prediction is 60% of that distance, so 0.60(32) = 19.2 cm.

per_choice.correct: The model predicts a dry-seed distance of 2 + 3(10) = 32 cm. The damp-seed prediction is 60% of that distance, so 0.60(32) = 19.2 cm.
per_choice.trap: 32 cm results from calculating the dry-seed prediction but failing to apply the 60% damp-seed factor; 16.8 cm can result from applying 60% to an incorrectly calculated dry distance of 28 cm; 35 cm comes from extending measured data rather than using the stated model.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, what was the estimated gross oxygen production, in mg/L, during the 20-min light exposure at 20 mg/L nitrate?
choices: 1.5 mg/L
2.0 mg/L
2.5 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers measured dissolved oxygen in algal cultures exposed to four nitrate concentrations for 20 min under constant light. Table 1 gives the oxygen concentration before and after the light exposure, while Figure 1 gives the respiration rate measured separately in darkness at each nitrate concentration. Net oxygen change equals gross photosynthetic production minus oxygen consumed by respiration; therefore, gross production can be estimated by adding dark respiration during the exposure to the observed oxygen increase. The 20-min exposure equals one-third of an hour.
items.explanation: At 20 mg/L nitrate, Table 1 shows an oxygen increase of 10.0 - 8.0 = 2.0 mg/L. Figure 1 gives a respiration rate of 0.5 mg/L/h, so respiration during one-third of an hour was 0.5/3 = 0.17 mg/L. Adding this to the observed increase gives approximately 2.17 mg/L of gross production.

per_choice.correct: At 20 mg/L nitrate, Table 1 shows an oxygen increase of 10.0 - 8.0 = 2.0 mg/L. Figure 1 gives a respiration rate of 0.5 mg/L/h, so respiration during one-third of an hour was 0.5/3 = 0.17 mg/L. Adding this to the observed increase gives approximately 2.17 mg/L of gross production.
per_choice.trap: 2.0 mg/L reports only the observed net increase and does not correct for respiration; 1.5 mg/L subtracts respiration from the oxygen increase; 2.5 mg/L adds the hourly respiration rate directly instead of scaling it to one-third of an hour.

items.stem: Which comparison of the measured water-loss values from 0.5 m/s to 4.0 m/s is most justified using Figure 1?
choices: Species A shows a fivefold increase, whereas Species B shows a 7.5-fold increase.
Both species show an eightfold increase because the model predicts an eightfold increase.
Species A shows a 7.5-fold increase, whereas Species B shows a fivefold increase.
Both species show the same fivefold increase because the wind-speed change is the same.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether a proportional model could predict water loss from leaves as wind speed increased. Leaves from two plant species were placed in a chamber at each wind speed, with temperature and relative humidity held constant; five leaves of each species were tested under each condition. Table 1 lists the chamber conditions and number of leaves tested. Figure 1 compares measured water loss with the model's predictions.
items.explanation: Figure 1 gives measured values of 11 to 55 mg/h for Species A and 8 to 60 mg/h for Species B. Thus Species A increases 55 / 11 = 5-fold, while Species B increases 60 / 8 = 7.5-fold.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 gives measured values of 11 to 55 mg/h for Species A and 8 to 60 mg/h for Species B. Thus Species A increases 55 / 11 = 5-fold, while Species B increases 60 / 8 = 7.5-fold.
per_choice.trap: Choice B substitutes the model prediction for the measured values; choice C swaps the two species' ratios; choice D assumes the same wind-speed change must produce the same measured ratio.

items.stem: If the Experiment 1 rate at 30°C continued for 15 min, what volume of CO2 would be collected, assuming the listed rate remained constant?
choices: 150 mL
180 mL
225 mL
450 mL
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how temperature affects fermentation by yeast in two experiments. Experiment 1 varied temperature and measured the rate of carbon dioxide production, whereas Experiment 2 used the same temperature settings and measured the time required to collect 50 mL of carbon dioxide. The experiments used the same yeast mass and pH, and the apparatus included a temperature-controlled bath and a gas-collection vessel. The researchers initially predicted that fermentation would become faster at every higher temperature tested.
items.explanation: Table 1 gives 15 mL/min at 30°C. Continuing that rate for 15 min gives 15 × 15 = 225 mL.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 gives 15 mL/min at 30°C. Continuing that rate for 15 min gives 15 × 15 = 225 mL.
per_choice.trap: 150 mL uses 10 min instead of 15 min; 180 mL uses the 12-min interval from the original calculation; 450 mL doubles the correct product.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Which result, if observed after extending the experiment beyond the time shown in Figure 1, would support the model's prediction about the eventual endpoint concentration?
choices: The TiO2 and no-TiO2 samples eventually reach the same dye concentration.
The two samples still have different concentrations at 15 minutes.
The TiO2 sample has a lower concentration during the first 15 minutes.
The no-TiO2 sample's concentration decreases during the 15-minute interval.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested a model of titanium dioxide (TiO2) photocatalysis by measuring the disappearance rate of an aqueous dye at several blue-light irradiances, with and without TiO2. The model predicts that TiO2 will increase the degradation rate at any nonzero irradiance but that TiO2 and the control will have equal rates in complete darkness. It also predicts that TiO2 changes the rate of degradation but not the eventual endpoint concentration, and a more specific version predicts that doubling irradiance from 20 to 40 mW/cm² will double the TiO2-catalyzed rate. Table 1 gives measured initial rates, and Figure 1 follows dye concentration for 15 minutes at 40 mW/cm².
items.explanation: The model predicts that TiO2 changes the rate but not the eventual endpoint concentration. Therefore, convergence to the same concentration after a sufficiently long exposure would support that prediction.

items.stem: Which quantity was deliberately varied among the flasks in the investigation, as shown by both Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: CO2 volume produced by the yeast
Temperature of the flasks
Sucrose concentration placed in each flask
Mass of yeast placed in each flask
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated whether the initial sucrose concentration affects carbon dioxide production by yeast. Each flask contained the same mass of yeast and liquid and was kept at 25°C; carbon dioxide volume was recorded during a 20-minute period. Table 1 summarizes the final measurement for each sucrose concentration, while Figure 1 shows how the measured gas volume changed during the period. The concentrations were selected to include a no-sucrose comparison and several sucrose treatments.
items.explanation: The sucrose concentration is the treatment that differs among the flasks and is used to organize the results in Table 1 and Figure 1. CO2 volume is the measured outcome, while temperature and yeast mass were held constant.

per_choice.correct: The sucrose concentration is the treatment that differs among the flasks and is used to organize the results in Table 1 and Figure 1. CO2 volume is the measured outcome, while temperature and yeast mass were held constant.
per_choice.trap: Choice A identifies the measured variable rather than the deliberately varied variable; choices B and D are controlled conditions.

items.stem:
According to Figure 1, at which pH is the difference between the rates of enzyme B and enzyme A greatest in favor of enzyme B?
  A. pH 6
  B. pH 7
  C. pH 8
  D. pH 9
choices: pH 6
pH 7
pH 8
pH 9
items.stimulus: Researchers compared the initial oxygen-production rates of enzyme A and enzyme B at several pH values. Each reaction took place in a flask containing substrate and buffer, and the gas produced was collected as shown in Figure 2; a second flask without enzyme measured background gas production. Table 1 gives enzyme A's measured rate and the background rate at selected pH values, while Figure 1 gives the rates for both enzymes across a wider pH range. Rates in the table and graph are reported in mL O2/min.
items.explanation: The B-minus-A differences are the negatives of the A-minus-B differences: -3, -9, -3, and 2 mL/min at pH 6, 7, 8, and 9, respectively. The greatest positive difference in favor of enzyme B is at pH 9.

per_choice.correct: The B-minus-A differences are the negatives of the A-minus-B differences: -3, -9, -3, and 2 mL/min at pH 6, 7, 8, and 9, respectively. The greatest positive difference in favor of enzyme B is at pH 9.
per_choice.trap: Choosing pH 7 follows the largest separation between the rates but fails to reverse the direction of the comparison; at pH 7, enzyme A is favored.

items.tests: Folding an added fact into what the passage already established.

items.stem:
At 6 min, which panel is predicted to produce the least electrical power according to Table 1 and Figure 1?
  A. Panel A
  B. Panels B and C equally
  C. Panel B
  D. Panel C
choices: Panel A
Panels B and C equally
Panel B
Panel C
items.stimulus: Researchers compared three photovoltaic panels while irradiance increased during a controlled test. Table 1 gives each panel’s collecting area and conversion efficiency, and Figure 1 gives irradiance during the measured interval. The model assumes that irradiance continues increasing linearly beyond the interval shown. It predicts electrical power with P = AηI, where A is area in m², η is efficiency, and I is irradiance in W/m²; efficiencies remain constant.
items.explanation: At the same predicted irradiance, compare the products of area and efficiency: Panel A has 0.374, Panel B has 0.360, and Panel C has 0.350. Therefore Panel C produces the least power at 6 min.

per_choice.correct: At the same predicted irradiance, compare the products of area and efficiency: Panel A has 0.374, Panel B has 0.360, and Panel C has 0.350. Therefore Panel C produces the least power at 6 min.
per_choice.trap: Panel B results from choosing the middle coefficient without comparing all three; the tie results from treating 0.360 and 0.350 as equal after excessive rounding.
