items.stem: Suppose the researchers discovered that the yeast volume in Trial 4 was accidentally 6 mL instead of the 5 mL listed in Table 1. Which comparison would then be least valid as evidence that caffeine alone caused the difference in Figure 1?
choices: The comparison of the 15 C and 35 C series in Figure 2
The comparison of Trial 2 with Trial 3
The comparison of Trial 1 with Trial 2
The comparison of Trial 1 with Trial 4
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether caffeine concentration affects carbon dioxide production by yeast fermenting sugar. Four trials used different caffeine concentrations, while the sugar concentration, yeast volume, and temperature were controlled as shown in Table 1. Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide production over 30 minutes for the Table 1 trials, and Figure 2 shows 30-minute carbon dioxide production at several temperatures and caffeine concentrations. The trial containing no caffeine served as the control.
items.explanation: Trial 1 and Trial 4 are intended to differ only in caffeine concentration, but the newly discovered yeast-volume difference adds a second changing factor. The Trial 1–Trial 4 comparison would therefore not isolate caffeine. The other listed comparisons do not involve the altered Trial 4 volume.

per_choice.trap: Choosing Trial 2 versus Trial 3 overlooks that both still use 5 mL of yeast; choosing the Figure 2 comparison confuses a temperature comparison with the contaminated Table 1 trial.

items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affected radish seedlings. They placed equal numbers of seeds in solutions with different NaCl concentrations while keeping seed type, solution volume, temperature, and light exposure constant. Table 1 shows the number of seeds germinated after 5 days, Figure 1 shows mean root length after 5 days, and Figure 2 shows the electrical conductivity of each solution. The NaCl concentration was set by the researchers, whereas germination, root length, and conductivity were measured.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: A solution has a conductivity of 5.95 mS/cm. Assuming the relationships in Figures 1 and 2 are linear between adjacent plotted concentrations, what mean root length would be predicted for seedlings in this solution?
choices: 8.0 mm
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affected radish seedlings. They placed equal numbers of seeds in solutions with different NaCl concentrations while keeping seed type, solution volume, temperature, and light exposure constant. Table 1 shows the number of seeds germinated after 5 days, Figure 1 shows mean root length after 5 days, and Figure 2 shows the electrical conductivity of each solution. The NaCl concentration was set by the researchers, whereas germination, root length, and conductivity were measured.
items.explanation: In Figure 2, 5.95 mS/cm is halfway between 4.8 at 4 g/L and 7.1 at 6 g/L, so the estimated concentration is 5 g/L. In Figure 1, root length halfway between 29 mm and 18 mm is 23.5 mm.

per_choice.correct: In Figure 2, 5.95 mS/cm is halfway between 4.8 at 4 g/L and 7.1 at 6 g/L, so the estimated concentration is 5 g/L. In Figure 1, root length halfway between 29 mm and 18 mm is 23.5 mm.
per_choice.trap: The endpoint values 18 mm and 29 mm come from Figure 1, but neither accounts for the intermediate concentration inferred from Figure 2.

items.stem: The researchers want to test whether the decrease in germination is related specifically to NaCl concentration rather than only to solution conductivity. Which additional treatment would provide the most direct comparison, using the existing data to select the treatment level?
choices: A 6 g/L NaCl solution with twice as many seeds, compared with the 6 g/L treatment
Distilled water with conductivity near 0.1 mS/cm, compared with the 0 g/L treatment
A non-NaCl electrolyte adjusted to conductivity near 7.1 mS/cm, compared with the 6 g/L NaCl treatment
A 4 g/L NaCl solution with conductivity near 4.8 mS/cm, compared with the 4 g/L treatment
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affected radish seedlings. They placed equal numbers of seeds in solutions with different NaCl concentrations while keeping seed type, solution volume, temperature, and light exposure constant. Table 1 shows the number of seeds germinated after 5 days, Figure 1 shows mean root length after 5 days, and Figure 2 shows the electrical conductivity of each solution. The NaCl concentration was set by the researchers, whereas germination, root length, and conductivity were measured.
items.explanation: Figure 2 shows that 6 g/L NaCl has conductivity near 7.1 mS/cm, while Table 1 gives its germination result. A different electrolyte at the same conductivity provides a comparison that changes the solute while matching conductivity.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 shows that 6 g/L NaCl has conductivity near 7.1 mS/cm, while Table 1 gives its germination result. A different electrolyte at the same conductivity provides a comparison that changes the solute while matching conductivity.
per_choice.trap: The first two choices merely repeat existing conditions, and the last changes sample size without separating NaCl concentration from conductivity.

items.stem: Why was a no-maltase control prepared at each pH instead of relying only on the initial measurements in Table 1? Use Table 1 and Figure 1.
choices: To account for both glucose present initially and glucose that appeared during incubation without maltase
To ensure that all pH samples began with exactly the same glucose concentration
To determine how much maltose solution was added to each reaction

items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects maltase conversion of maltose to glucose. items.stem: Why did the researchers measure glucose before incubation, even though Figure 1 already includes a no-maltase control at each pH? Use Table 1 and Figure 1.
choices: To establish the starting amount so that increases during incubation could be calculated separately from preexisting glucose
To determine whether the reaction mixtures were held at the same temperature during incubation
To show that the enzyme mixtures and control mixtures had equal final glucose concentrations
To identify the pH at which maltase produced the most glucose without using the final measurements
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects maltase conversion of maltose to glucose. At each pH, equal volumes of substrate and maltase solution were mixed, while a matched mixture without maltase served as a control. Glucose concentration was measured before incubation and after 10 minutes; a stopping reagent was added immediately after the 10-minute measurement. Table 1 shows initial glucose concentrations, Figure 1 shows final concentrations for enzyme and control mixtures, and Figure 2 shows glucose production attributed to maltase after correction for background change.
items.explanation: The initial readings in Table 1 allow each final reading in Figure 1 to be converted into a change. The control then indicates how much of that change occurred without maltase; neither step replaces the other.

items.stem: What comparison would be most directly compromised if the stopping reagent were omitted after the 10-minute measurement? Use the procedure and Figure 2.
choices: The ability to record the initial glucose concentrations listed in Table 1
The ability to prepare mixtures with equal volumes of substrate and maltase
The comparison of glucose produced during an equal 10-minute interval at the different pH values
The comparison of the starting glucose concentration with the final glucose concentration
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how pH affects maltase conversion of maltose to glucose. At each pH, equal volumes of substrate and maltase solution were mixed, while a matched mixture without maltase served as a control. Glucose concentration was measured before incubation and after 10 minutes; a stopping reagent was added immediately after the 10-minute measurement. Table 1 shows initial glucose concentrations, Figure 1 shows final concentrations for enzyme and control mixtures, and Figure 2 shows glucose production attributed to maltase after correction for background change.
items.explanation: The stopping reagent prevents the enzyme reaction from continuing while samples are being processed. Without it, samples could react for different additional times, so the corrected production values in Figure 2 would no longer represent equal 10-minute intervals.

items.tests: Why a particular procedure or measurement was included.

items.stem: If a further trial used 0.30 mg/L CuSO4, which pair of values would be the best estimate for the growth rate and chlorophyll production, respectively? Use Table 1 and Figure 2.
choices: 6 cells/day and 31 mg/L
9 cells/day and 24.5 mg/L
12 cells/day and 18 mg/L
15 cells/day and 38 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how copper sulfate concentration affected a freshwater algae culture. Cultures were exposed to the listed concentrations, and investigators measured growth rate, survival, cell count over time, and chlorophyll production. Table 1 shows average growth rate and survival after 7 days; Figure 1 shows cell counts for selected concentrations; and Figure 2 shows chlorophyll production after 30 minutes. For an untested concentration between two tested concentrations, the researchers estimated values by interpolating between the neighboring results.
items.explanation: At 0.30 mg/L, the growth-rate estimate halfway between 12 and 6 is 9 cells/day. The chlorophyll estimate halfway between 31 and 18 is 24.5 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: At 0.30 mg/L, the growth-rate estimate halfway between 12 and 6 is 9 cells/day. The chlorophyll estimate halfway between 31 and 18 is 24.5 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: The other choices combine values from the tested 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4 mg/L rows instead of interpolating between the two neighboring concentrations.

items.tests: Predicting the result of a trial that was not run, from the pattern that was.

items.stem: In the 0.30 mg/L further trial, what pair of results would be expected at day 6: cell count and growth rate, respectively? Use Figure 1 and Table 1.
choices: 2.7 and 6 cells/day
3.25 and 9 cells/day
3.8 and 12 cells/day
5.0 and 15 cells/day
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how copper sulfate concentration affected a freshwater algae culture. Cultures were exposed to the listed concentrations, and investigators measured growth rate, survival, cell count over time, and chlorophyll production. Table 1 shows average growth rate and survival after 7 days; Figure 1 shows cell counts for selected concentrations; and Figure 2 shows chlorophyll production after 30 minutes. For an untested concentration between two tested concentrations, the researchers estimated values by interpolating between the neighboring results.
items.explanation: At day 6, the cell count is estimated halfway between the 0.2 mg/L value of 3.8 and the 0.4 mg/L value of 2.7, giving 3.25. Table 1 similarly gives a growth-rate estimate halfway between 12 and 6, or 9 cells/day.

per_choice.correct: At day 6, the cell count is estimated halfway between the 0.2 mg/L value of 3.8 and the 0.4 mg/L value of 2.7, giving 3.25. Table 1 similarly gives a growth-rate estimate halfway between 12 and 6, or 9 cells/day.
per_choice.trap: Each incorrect pair uses a complete set of values associated with a tested concentration, but not with the interpolated 0.30 mg/L condition.

items.tests: Predicting the result of a trial that was not run, from the pattern that was.

items.stem: The researchers hypothesized that increasing CuSO4 concentration would lower both survival and chlorophyll production. Which pair of results from a 0.30 mg/L further trial would most strongly contradict that hypothesis? Use Table 1 and Figure 2.
choices: 60% survival and 31 mg/L chlorophyll
71% survival and 24.5 mg/L chlorophyll
82% survival and 24.5 mg/L chlorophyll
91% survival and 38 mg/L chlorophyll
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how copper sulfate concentration affected a freshwater algae culture. Cultures were exposed to the listed concentrations, and investigators measured growth rate, survival, cell count over time, and chlorophyll production. Table 1 shows average growth rate and survival after 7 days; Figure 1 shows cell counts for selected concentrations; and Figure 2 shows chlorophyll production after 30 minutes. For an untested concentration between two tested concentrations, the researchers estimated values by interpolating between the neighboring results.
items.explanation: At 0.30 mg/L, both measures should fall between their 0.2 and 0.4 mg/L values. A result of 91% survival and 38 mg/L chlorophyll is higher than the expected intermediate values and matches the much lower-concentration 0.1 mg/L results, strongly contradicting the declining trend.

per_choice.correct: At 0.30 mg/L, both measures should fall between their 0.2 and 0.4 mg/L values. A result of 91% survival and 38 mg/L chlorophyll is higher than the expected intermediate values and matches the much lower-concentration 0.1 mg/L results, strongly contradicting the declining trend.
per_choice.trap: The first choice uses a survival value from 0.4 mg/L with a chlorophyll value from 0.2 mg/L; the middle choices are close to or equal to expected intermediate results rather than contradicting the trend.

items.stem: Suppose the 0.30 mg/L further trial began with 2.4 × 10^5 cells/mL instead of the 2.0 × 10^5 cells/mL used in Figure 1. If cell counts scale proportionally with the starting count, what day-6 count should be predicted? Use Figure 1 and the interpolation rule stated in the passage.
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how copper sulfate concentration affected a freshwater algae culture. Cultures were exposed to the listed concentrations, and investigators measured growth rate, survival, cell count over time, and chlorophyll production. Table 1 shows average growth rate and survival after 7 days; Figure 1 shows cell counts for selected concentrations; and Figure 2 shows chlorophyll production after 30 minutes. For an untested concentration between two tested concentrations, the researchers estimated values by interpolating between the neighboring results.
items.explanation: Interpolating Figure 1 gives 3.25 × 10^5/mL at day 6 for a starting count of 2.0 × 10^5/mL. Because 2.4 is 1.2 times 2.0, the adjusted prediction is 3.25 × 1.2 = 3.9 × 10^5/mL.

per_choice.correct: Interpolating Figure 1 gives 3.25 × 10^5/mL at day 6 for a starting count of 2.0 × 10^5/mL. Because 2.4 is 1.2 times 2.0, the adjusted prediction is 3.25 × 1.2 = 3.9 × 10^5/mL.
per_choice.trap: 3.25 ignores the changed starting count, 3.8 uses the tested 0.2 mg/L series, and 5.0 uses the day-6 control value.

items.stem: Considering both Table 1 and Figure 1, which evaluation of the researchers' hypothesis is best supported?
choices: The germination portion is contradicted, but the dry-mass portion is supported because the longest germination time occurred at the highest salt concentration.
The hypothesis is untested because the data do not include a 0 g/L comparison.

items.stem: Using the germination percentages in Table 1 and the per-seed dry masses in Figure 1, how much less total dry mass would be expected from 100 seeds at 4 g/L than from 100 seeds at 0 g/L?
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of bean seedlings. Seeds were placed in solutions containing 0, 2, 4, or 6 g/L sodium chloride, and measurements were made after 10 days. The researchers hypothesized that salinity would reduce the percentage of seeds that germinated but would not affect the dry mass of seedlings that did germinate. Table 1 gives germination results and mean time to germination, Figure 1 gives mean dry mass per germinated seed, and Figure 2 gives the root-to-shoot mass ratio at each salt concentration.
items.explanation: At 0 g/L, 96 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 96 × 0.84 = 80.64 g. At 4 g/L, 75 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 75 × 0.61 = 45.75 g. The difference is 80.64 − 45.75 = 34.89 g.

per_choice.correct: At 0 g/L, 96 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 96 × 0.84 = 80.64 g. At 4 g/L, 75 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 75 × 0.61 = 45.75 g. The difference is 80.64 − 45.75 = 34.89 g.
per_choice.trap: 22.08 g results from using the 0 g/L germination percentage with the 4 g/L mass. 45.75 g is only the calculated 4 g/L total, and 80.64 g is only the calculated control total.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which comparison between the displays provides the strongest support for Scientist 2's claim that matching acclimation and test temperatures improves performance?
choices: At 15 C, fish acclimated to 10 C survived better than fish acclimated to 20 C in Figure 2.
At 25 C, fish acclimated to 20 C consumed less oxygen than fish acclimated to 10 C in Table 1.
At both 10 C and 25 C, the fish acclimated closer to the test temperature had both the greater swimming speed in Figure 1 and the greater survival in Figure 2.
At 10 C, fish acclimated to 10 C consumed less oxygen than fish acclimated to 20 C in Table 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested juvenile fish that had been acclimated for 2 weeks to either 10 C or 20 C, then measured each group at 10, 15, 20, or 25 C. Table 1 shows oxygen consumption, Figure 1 shows critical swimming speed after 7 days at the test temperature, and Figure 2 shows survival after a sudden 6-hour exposure. Scientist 1 argues that current water temperature alone determines performance, whereas Scientist 2 argues that performance depends mainly on the match between acclimation temperature and test temperature. The scientists used the same temperature values in all three displays.
items.explanation: At both extreme test temperatures, the group whose acclimation temperature was closer to the test temperature had the higher swimming speed and survival. The other choices describe only one measurement or one temperature.

per_choice.correct: At both extreme test temperatures, the group whose acclimation temperature was closer to the test temperature had the higher swimming speed and survival. The other choices describe only one measurement or one temperature.
per_choice.trap: Choosing a true oxygen-consumption or single-temperature comparison instead of the paired pattern across both performance displays.

items.tests: Where two scientists agree or disagree, and what evidence each relies on.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, what was the difference between the groups in oxygen consumed per centimeter per second of swimming at 25 C, rounded to the nearest 0.01 mg/cm?
choices: 0.02 mg/cm
0.04 mg/cm
0.07 mg/cm
0.12 mg/cm
items.stimulus: Researchers tested juvenile fish that had been acclimated for 2 weeks to either 10 C or 20 C, then measured each group at 10, 15, 20, or 25 C. Table 1 shows oxygen consumption, Figure 1 shows critical swimming speed after 7 days at the test temperature, and Figure 2 shows survival after a sudden 6-hour exposure. Scientist 1 argues that current water temperature alone determines performance, whereas Scientist 2 argues that performance depends mainly on the match between acclimation temperature and test temperature. The scientists used the same temperature values in all three displays.
items.explanation: For fish acclimated to 10 C, the ratio was 8.0/44 = 0.182 mg/cm. For fish acclimated to 20 C, it was 7.0/49 = 0.143 mg/cm. The difference is 0.039, which rounds to 0.04 mg/cm.

per_choice.correct: For fish acclimated to 10 C, the ratio was 8.0/44 = 0.182 mg/cm. For fish acclimated to 20 C, it was 7.0/49 = 0.143 mg/cm. The difference is 0.039, which rounds to 0.04 mg/cm.
per_choice.trap: Using the oxygen-consumption difference alone, using swimming-speed difference alone, or dividing the values in the wrong direction.

items.tests: Where two scientists agree or disagree, and what evidence each relies on.

items.stem: At which test temperature do the two acclimation groups show the greatest difference in swimming speed while also showing a survival difference tied for the greatest difference?
items.stimulus: Researchers tested juvenile fish that had been acclimated for 2 weeks to either 10 C or 20 C, then measured each group at 10, 15, 20, or 25 C. Table 1 shows oxygen consumption, Figure 1 shows critical swimming speed after 7 days at the test temperature, and Figure 2 shows survival after a sudden 6-hour exposure. Scientist 1 argues that current water temperature alone determines performance, whereas Scientist 2 argues that performance depends mainly on the match between acclimation temperature and test temperature. The scientists used the same temperature values in all three displays.
items.explanation: Swimming-speed differences are 7, 3, 2, and 5 cm/s at 10, 15, 20, and 25 C, respectively. Survival differences are 18, 8, 2, and 18 percentage points, so 10 C has the largest speed difference and is tied for the largest survival difference.

per_choice.correct: Swimming-speed differences are 7, 3, 2, and 5 cm/s at 10, 15, 20, and 25 C, respectively. Survival differences are 18, 8, 2, and 18 percentage points, so 10 C has the largest speed difference and is tied for the largest survival difference.
per_choice.trap: Selecting 25 C because it also has an 18-point survival difference, while overlooking that the swimming-speed difference is larger at 10 C.

items.tests: Where two scientists agree or disagree, and what evidence each relies on.

items.stem: Which conclusion best reconciles all 3 displays without fully accepting either scientist's claim?
choices: Test temperature affects oxygen consumption in both groups, but acclimation temperature has no consistent relation to swimming speed or survival.

Both test temperature and acclimation history influence the results; performance advantages generally occur when acclimation and test temperatures are similar, while oxygen consumption also changes with test temperature.
Acclimation temperature affects swimming speed and survival, but test temperature has no effect on oxygen consumption.
Higher oxygen consumption consistently causes lower swimming speed and survival, regardless of acclimation temperature.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested juvenile fish that had been acclimated for 2 weeks to either 10 C or 20 C, then measured each group at 10, 15, 20, or 25 C. Table 1 shows oxygen consumption, Figure 1 shows critical swimming speed after 7 days at the test temperature, and Figure 2 shows survival after a sudden 6-hour exposure. Scientist 1 argues that current water temperature alone determines performance, whereas Scientist 2 argues that performance depends mainly on the match between acclimation temperature and test temperature. The scientists used the same temperature values in all three displays.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows oxygen consumption changing with test temperature, while Figures 1 and 2 show that acclimation history changes performance at the same test temperature. The best-supported interpretation therefore includes both factors and the temperature-match pattern.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows oxygen consumption changing with test temperature, while Figures 1 and 2 show that acclimation history changes performance at the same test temperature. The best-supported interpretation therefore includes both factors and the temperature-match pattern.
per_choice.trap: Treating one display as decisive, or confusing a repeated association between oxygen use and performance with proof that oxygen use is the sole cause.

items.stem: Which conclusion about the developers' claim that the model is practically usable at either tested temperature is best supported by Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2?
choices: The claim is supported only at 15°C because Figure 2 shows errors no greater than 10 points.
The claim is supported at 25°C, but not at 15°C, because the 15°C errors exceed the stated limit at every pH.
The claim is supported at both temperatures because every 25°C discrepancy is 5 points or less.
The claim is unsupported at both temperatures because the model does not exactly match any measured value.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested a model intended to predict the percentage of nitrate removed by a biological filter at different influent pH values. Filter columns were operated at 15°C and 25°C, and nitrate removal was measured after steady operation. Table 1 shows the measured mean removal at each temperature, Figure 1 compares the model predictions with the 25°C measurements, and Figure 2 shows the model's absolute error for the 15°C measurements. The model developers considered an absolute error of 5 percentage points or less acceptable for practical use.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows 25°C discrepancies of 1, 2, 4, and 3 points, all within 5. Figure 2 shows 15°C errors of 7, 10, 9, and 7 points, all above the acceptable limit.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows 25°C discrepancies of 1, 2, 4, and 3 points, all within 5. Figure 2 shows 15°C errors of 7, 10, 9, and 7 points, all above the acceptable limit.
per_choice.trap: A student may treat an error of 10 points as acceptable because it is close to the 5-point threshold, or may reject the model for failing to match values exactly.

items.tests: Whether a conclusion follows from the data, or over-reaches it.

items.stem: Suppose a new 15°C column at pH 8 produced 68% removal. Relative to the existing evidence in Figure 1 and Figure 2, what would this new result imply under the 5-point acceptance rule?
choices: It would show that the model predicts 15°C removal exactly, because Figure 2 already reports a 9-point error at pH 8.
It would strengthen the model's 15°C evaluation to acceptable, because 68% is closer to the 15°C mean than the model prediction is.
It would improve agreement at pH 8 but still fail the rule, because the model predicts 74%, making the new error 6 points.
It would weaken the model, because 68% is farther from the model prediction than the existing 15°C mean.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested a model intended to predict the percentage of nitrate removed by a biological filter at different influent pH values. Filter columns were operated at 15°C and 25°C, and nitrate removal was measured after steady operation. Table 1 shows the measured mean removal at each temperature, Figure 1 compares the model predictions with the 25°C measurements, and Figure 2 shows the model's absolute error for the 15°C measurements. The model developers considered an absolute error of 5 percentage points or less acceptable for practical use.
items.explanation: Figure 1 gives a model prediction of 74% at pH 8. The new value of 68% differs by 6 points, so it is closer than the existing 15°C mean error of 9 points shown in Figure 2, but it remains outside the 5-point acceptable range.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 gives a model prediction of 74% at pH 8. The new value of 68% differs by 6 points, so it is closer than the existing 15°C mean error of 9 points shown in Figure 2, but it remains outside the 5-point acceptable range.
per_choice.trap: A student may call the result acceptable merely because it improves on the 9-point error, rather than comparing it with the separate 5-point criterion.

items.tests: Whether a conclusion follows from the data, or over-reaches it.

items.stem: Using the stated length relationship and the 1.00-m, 0.50-kg value in Table 1, what period does the model predict for a 0.50-kg pendulum that is 1.50 m long?
items.stimulus: Researchers tested pendulums with bob masses of 0.20 kg and 0.50 kg at three lengths, timing 20 complete swings and dividing by 20 to obtain the period. The stated model predicts that period is proportional to the square root of length and is independent of bob mass; it also predicts that period is proportional to 1 divided by the square root of gravitational acceleration. Table 1 lists measured periods, Figure 1 compares the two masses, and Figure 2 shows the percent by which the 0.50-kg measurements exceeded the model prediction at each tested length.
items.explanation: The model scales period by the square root of length, so the prediction is 2.01 × √(1.50/1.00), which is approximately 2.46 s.

per_choice.correct: The model scales period by the square root of length, so the prediction is 2.01 × √(1.50/1.00), which is approximately 2.46 s.
per_choice.trap: 2.01 s uses the measured value from the 1.00-m row without extending it; 2.84 s is the prediction for 2.00 m, and 3.02 s multiplies the period directly by 1.50 instead of using the square-root relationship.

items.stem: For pendulums of both masses at a length of 1.50 m, what difference between their model-predicted periods should be expected? Use the mass comparison in Figure 1 together with the stated model.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested pendulums with bob masses of 0.20 kg and 0.50 kg at three lengths, timing 20 complete swings and dividing by 20 to obtain the period. The stated model predicts that period is proportional to the square root of length and is independent of bob mass; it also predicts that period is proportional to 1 divided by the square root of gravitational acceleration. Table 1 lists measured periods, Figure 1 compares the two masses, and Figure 2 shows the percent by which the 0.50-kg measurements exceeded the model prediction at each tested length.
items.explanation: The model states that period is independent of bob mass. Therefore, even though Figure 1 shows small measured differences at the tested lengths, the two model predictions at 1.50 m should be equal, with a difference of 0.00 s.

per_choice.correct: The model states that period is independent of bob mass. Therefore, even though Figure 1 shows small measured differences at the tested lengths, the two model predictions at 1.50 m should be equal, with a difference of 0.00 s.
per_choice.trap: The nonzero choices come from treating measured mass differences in Table 1 or Figure 1 as part of the model rather than recognizing that the model explicitly removes mass as a variable.

items.stem: If the 1.50-m, 0.50-kg pendulum were tested on the Moon, where gravitational acceleration is 1.6 m/s² instead of 9.8 m/s², what period would the model predict?
items.stimulus: Researchers tested pendulums with bob masses of 0.20 kg and 0.50 kg at three lengths, timing 20 complete swings and dividing by 20 to obtain the period. The stated model predicts that period is proportional to the square root of length and is independent of bob mass; it also predicts that period is proportional to 1 divided by the square root of gravitational acceleration. Table 1 lists measured periods, Figure 1 compares the two masses, and Figure 2 shows the percent by which the 0.50-kg measurements exceeded the model prediction at each tested length.
items.explanation: The terrestrial prediction for 1.50 m is about 2.46 s. Because period is proportional to 1/√g, the lunar prediction is 2.46 × √(9.8/1.6), or approximately 6.08 s.

per_choice.correct: The terrestrial prediction for 1.50 m is about 2.46 s. Because period is proportional to 1/√g, the lunar prediction is 2.46 × √(9.8/1.6), or approximately 6.08 s.
per_choice.trap: 2.46 s applies the length prediction but ignores the changed gravitational acceleration; 3.94 s uses the acceleration ratio without the required square root, and 15.13 s uses the inverse relationship incorrectly.

items.tests: Using a stated model to predict an outcome outside the data shown.

items.stem: A new 1.50-m, 0.50-kg pendulum gives one of the following periods. Which result would most strongly challenge the model's length relationship rather than being comparable to the deviations shown in Figure 2?
items.stimulus: Researchers tested pendulums with bob masses of 0.20 kg and 0.50 kg at three lengths, timing 20 complete swings and dividing by 20 to obtain the period. The stated model predicts that period is proportional to the square root of length and is independent of bob mass; it also predicts that period is proportional to 1 divided by the square root of gravitational acceleration. Table 1 lists measured periods, Figure 1 compares the two masses, and Figure 2 shows the percent by which the 0.50-kg measurements exceeded the model prediction at each tested length.
items.explanation: The model predicts about 2.46 s at 1.50 m. Figure 2 shows that the largest tested excess above the model is 4%, which would correspond to about 2.56 s; 3.20 s is about 30% above the prediction and would be far outside the displayed deviations.

per_choice.correct: The model predicts about 2.46 s at 1.50 m. Figure 2 shows that the largest tested excess above the model is 4%, which would correspond to about 2.56 s; 3.20 s is about 30% above the prediction and would be far outside the displayed deviations.
per_choice.trap: 2.46 s is the model prediction, while 2.50 s and 2.56 s are close enough to the prediction to resemble the observed measurement deviations; selecting one of them treats ordinary experimental variation as a model failure.

items.tests: Using a stated model to predict an outcome outside the data shown.

items.stem: Which statement is consistent with the results shown in Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2?
choices: Film A was stronger at every humidity, while Film B had lower water uptake and lower mass loss at every humidity.
Film B was stronger at every humidity and had lower mass loss, while Film A had lower water uptake at every humidity.
Film B was stronger at every humidity, while Film B had lower water uptake and Film A had lower mass loss at every humidity.
Film A was stronger at every humidity and had lower water uptake, while Film B had lower mass loss at every humidity.
items.stimulus: Researchers compared biodegradable Film A and Film B after conditioning samples at 20%, 50%, or 80% relative humidity. Table 1 shows tensile strength after conditioning, Figure 1 shows water uptake during conditioning, and Figure 2 shows mass lost after the conditioned samples were stored for 30 days. All three displays use the same humidity levels and distinguish between the two films.
items.explanation: Table 1 gives Film A the greater strength at 20%, 50%, and 80%. Figure 1 gives Film B the lower water uptake at all three humidities, and Figure 2 gives Film B the lower mass loss at all three humidities.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 gives Film A the greater strength at 20%, 50%, and 80%. Figure 1 gives Film B the lower water uptake at all three humidities, and Figure 2 gives Film B the lower mass loss at all three humidities.
per_choice.trap: The other choices correctly identify one comparison but reverse the film identities for either water uptake, mass loss, or strength.

items.stem: Which statement about the changes from 20% to 80% relative humidity is consistent with the data for both films?
choices: For each film, the percentage increase in mass loss was greater than the percentage increase in water uptake, and both exceeded the percentage decrease in tensile strength.
For each film, the percentage decrease in tensile strength was greater than the percentage increases in water uptake and mass loss.
For each film, the percentage increase in water uptake was greater than the percentage increase in mass loss, while the strength decrease was smallest.
For each film, the percentage changes in tensile strength, water uptake, and mass loss were approximately equal.
items.stimulus: Researchers compared biodegradable Film A and Film B after conditioning samples at 20%, 50%, or 80% relative humidity. Table 1 shows tensile strength after conditioning, Figure 1 shows water uptake during conditioning, and Figure 2 shows mass lost after the conditioned samples were stored for 30 days. All three displays use the same humidity levels and distinguish between the two films.
items.explanation: For Film A, mass loss increased from 2% to 11% (450%), water uptake from 4% to 18% (350%), and strength decreased by about 43%. For Film B, mass loss increased from 1% to 9% (800%), water uptake from 3% to 15% (400%), and strength decreased by about 47%. Thus, for both films, mass-loss percentage change was greatest, water-uptake change was next, and strength change was smallest.

per_choice.correct: For Film A, mass loss increased from 2% to 11% (450%), water uptake from 4% to 18% (350%), and strength decreased by about 43%. For Film B, mass loss increased from 1% to 9% (800%), water uptake from 3% to 15% (400%), and strength decreased by about 47%. Thus, for both films, mass-loss percentage change was greatest, water-uptake change was next, and strength change was smallest.
per_choice.trap: A student may compare absolute differences instead of percentage changes, or may use the order for one film while ignoring whether it also holds for the other film.

items.tests: Finding one value in a table or off a graph, with the right row, column and units.

items.stem: According to Figure 1, at which temperature did Trial B produce more CO2 than Trial A by the greatest amount?
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affected fermentation by mixing equal amounts of yeast, sugar, and water. The mixtures were maintained at four temperatures, and carbon dioxide production and acidity were measured. Table 1 shows measurements after 20 minutes, Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide measurements from two trials at each temperature, and Figure 2 shows the time required to reach the peak carbon dioxide production rate.
items.explanation: Trial B exceeded Trial A by 2 mL at 15 C, 6 mL at 25 C, 1 mL at 35 C, and 2 mL at 45 C. The greatest difference was at 25 C.

per_choice.correct: Trial B exceeded Trial A by 2 mL at 15 C, 6 mL at 25 C, 1 mL at 35 C, and 2 mL at 45 C. The greatest difference was at 25 C.
per_choice.trap: The student may choose 35 C because it has the greatest overall CO2 values, even though the difference between the trials is smallest there.

items.tests: Finding one value in a table or off a graph, with the right row, column and units.

items.stem: At 35 C, which statement correctly gives the CO2 production in Table 1 and the peak time in Figure 2?
choices: 35 mL of CO2 and 10 min
35 mL of CO2 and 14 min
18 mL of CO2 and 10 min
18 mL of CO2 and 14 min
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affected fermentation by mixing equal amounts of yeast, sugar, and water. The mixtures were maintained at four temperatures, and carbon dioxide production and acidity were measured. Table 1 shows measurements after 20 minutes, Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide measurements from two trials at each temperature, and Figure 2 shows the time required to reach the peak carbon dioxide production rate.
items.explanation: The 35 C row in Table 1 gives 35 mL of CO2, and the 35 C bar in Figure 2 gives a peak time of 10 min.

per_choice.correct: The 35 C row in Table 1 gives 35 mL of CO2, and the 35 C bar in Figure 2 gives a peak time of 10 min.

items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affected fermentation by mixing equal amounts of yeast, sugar, and water. Table 1 shows measurements after 20 minutes, Figure 1 shows carbon dioxide measurements from two trials at each temperature, and Figure 2 shows the time required to reach the peak carbon dioxide production rate.
items.explanation: Figure 2 shows 16 min at 25 C and 14 min at 45 C. Therefore, the peak time at 45 C was 2 min shorter.

items.stem: According to Table 1, what is the estimated nitrate concentration in the sand-column effluent at 15 min?
choices: 56 mg/L
60 mg/L
62 mg/L
68 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers measured nitrate concentration in water flowing through laboratory columns packed with sand, loam, or clay. Water samples were collected at several times during a 30-minute test. Table 1 gives measurements from the sand column, Figure 1 shows the loam-column measurements, and Figure 2 shows the clay-column measurements. For estimates between plotted times, assume the concentration changes at a constant rate between adjacent measurements.
items.explanation: At 15 min, the estimate is halfway between the 10-min value of 68 mg/L and the 20-min value of 56 mg/L: (68 + 56) / 2 = 62 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: At 15 min, the estimate is halfway between the 10-min value of 68 mg/L and the 20-min value of 56 mg/L: (68 + 56) / 2 = 62 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: 56 mg/L is the 20-min sand value, while 68 mg/L is the 10-min sand value; 60 mg/L comes from using a value associated with another display or interval.

items.tests: Estimating between plotted points, or beyond them, without over-reaching.

items.stem: Using Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2, and assuming that each column's most recent 10-minute trend continues to 40 min, which pair of columns would have the most similar nitrate concentrations at 40 min?
choices: Clay and sand
Loam and sand
Clay and loam
The concentrations cannot be compared
items.stimulus: Researchers measured nitrate concentration in water flowing through laboratory columns packed with sand, loam, or clay. Water samples were collected at several times during a 30-minute test. Table 1 gives measurements from the sand column, Figure 1 shows the loam-column measurements, and Figure 2 shows the clay-column measurements. For estimates between plotted times, assume the concentration changes at a constant rate between adjacent measurements.
items.explanation: From 20 to 30 min, sand decreases by 12 mg/L, loam by 8 mg/L, and clay by 10 mg/L. Extrapolating gives 32 mg/L for sand, 48 mg/L for loam, and 25 mg/L for clay, so clay and sand are closest.

per_choice.correct: From 20 to 30 min, sand decreases by 12 mg/L, loam by 8 mg/L, and clay by 10 mg/L. Extrapolating gives 32 mg/L for sand, 48 mg/L for loam, and 25 mg/L for clay, so clay and sand are closest.
per_choice.trap: Choosing loam and sand results from noticing that both have relatively gradual declines without extrapolating their separate 30-to-40-minute values.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, what is the estimated difference between the nitrate concentrations for the sand and loam columns at 25 min?
choices: 4 mg/L
8 mg/L
10 mg/L
14 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers measured nitrate concentration in water flowing through laboratory columns packed with sand, loam, or clay. Water samples were collected at several times during a 30-minute test. Table 1 gives measurements from the sand column, Figure 1 shows the loam-column measurements, and Figure 2 shows the clay-column measurements. For estimates between plotted times, assume the concentration changes at a constant rate between adjacent measurements.
items.explanation: At 25 min, sand is halfway between 56 and 44 mg/L, or 50 mg/L. Loam is halfway between 64 and 56 mg/L, or 60 mg/L. The difference is 10 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: At 25 min, sand is halfway between 56 and 44 mg/L, or 50 mg/L. Loam is halfway between 64 and 56 mg/L, or 60 mg/L. The difference is 10 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: 8 mg/L is the loam decrease from 20 to 30 min, and 14 mg/L can result from comparing values from mismatched times or columns.

items.stem: A new soil column has nitrate concentrations of 70 mg/L at 10 min and 58 mg/L at 20 min. At 15 min, its estimated concentration would be closest to the value for which column? Use Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2 for comparison.
choices: The clay column
The sand column
It would be equally close to all three
The loam column
items.stimulus: Researchers measured nitrate concentration in water flowing through laboratory columns packed with sand, loam, or clay. Water samples were collected at several times during a 30-minute test. Table 1 gives measurements from the sand column, Figure 1 shows the loam-column measurements, and Figure 2 shows the clay-column measurements. For estimates between plotted times, assume the concentration changes at a constant rate between adjacent measurements.
items.explanation: The new column's midpoint estimate is (70 + 58) / 2 = 64 mg/L. At 15 min, sand is about 62 mg/L, loam about 68 mg/L, and clay about 52.5 mg/L, making the sand value closest.

per_choice.correct: The new column's midpoint estimate is (70 + 58) / 2 = 64 mg/L. At 15 min, sand is about 62 mg/L, loam about 68 mg/L, and clay about 52.5 mg/L, making the sand value closest.
per_choice.trap: Choosing loam results from comparing 64 mg/L with the 20-min loam value of 64 mg/L instead of interpolating the loam value at 15 min.

items.tests: Estimating between plotted points, or beyond them, without over-reaching.

items.stem: According to Figure 1, how much greater is the usable capacity at 30°C than at 40°C?
choices: 70 mAh
90 mAh
100 mAh
items.stimulus: Researchers tested rechargeable batteries at four temperatures. Identical batteries were allowed to reach thermal equilibrium before their average voltage, usable capacity, and internal resistance were measured. Table 1 shows average voltage at each temperature, Figure 1 shows usable capacity, and Figure 2 shows internal resistance; all measurements are organized by temperature.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows 1,000 mAh at 30°C and 910 mAh at 40°C; 1,000 − 910 = 90 mAh.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows 1,000 mAh at 30°C and 910 mAh at 40°C; 1,000 − 910 = 90 mAh.
per_choice.trap: A student may compare the 30°C value with the 20°C value or report the 30°C capacity itself.

items.stem: At the temperature where Figure 2 shows the lowest internal resistance, what usable capacity is shown in Figure 1?
choices: 820 mAh
910 mAh
940 mAh
items.stimulus: Researchers tested rechargeable batteries at four temperatures. Identical batteries were allowed to reach thermal equilibrium before their average voltage, usable capacity, and internal resistance were measured. Table 1 shows average voltage at each temperature, Figure 1 shows usable capacity, and Figure 2 shows internal resistance; all measurements are organized by temperature.
items.explanation: The lowest resistance in Figure 2 is 0.39 ohm at 30°C. Figure 1 gives a capacity of 1,000 mAh at 30°C.

per_choice.correct: The lowest resistance in Figure 2 is 0.39 ohm at 30°C. Figure 1 gives a capacity of 1,000 mAh at 30°C.
per_choice.trap: A student may select the lowest resistance value's position as though it were a capacity, or use the capacity at 20°C, where resistance is also below 0.50 ohm.

items.stem: Using the approximation energy = capacity × average voltage, how much more energy would the battery provide at 20°C than at 40°C?
choices: 29 mWh
54 mWh
90 mWh
items.stimulus: Researchers tested rechargeable batteries at four temperatures. Identical batteries were allowed to reach thermal equilibrium before their average voltage, usable capacity, and internal resistance were measured. Table 1 shows average voltage at each temperature, Figure 1 shows usable capacity, and Figure 2 shows internal resistance; all measurements are organized by temperature.
items.explanation: At 20°C, Figure 1 and Table 1 give 940 mAh and 1.50 V, or 1,410 mWh. At 40°C, they give 910 mAh and 1.49 V, or about 1,356 mWh. The difference is about 54 mWh.

per_choice.correct: At 20°C, Figure 1 and Table 1 give 940 mAh and 1.50 V, or 1,410 mWh. At 40°C, they give 910 mAh and 1.49 V, or about 1,356 mWh. The difference is about 54 mWh.
per_choice.trap: A student may subtract capacities only, obtaining 30 mAh, or use the 30°C voltage from Table 1 with the 40°C capacity.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: A sensor requires a battery with capacity greater than 900 mAh and internal resistance less than 0.50 ohm. Based on Figures 1 and 2, at which tested temperatures would the battery meet both requirements?
choices: 10°C only
20°C and 30°C only
30°C and 40°C only
items.stimulus: Researchers tested rechargeable batteries at four temperatures. Identical batteries were allowed to reach thermal equilibrium before their average voltage, usable capacity, and internal resistance were measured. Table 1 shows average voltage at each temperature, Figure 1 shows usable capacity, and Figure 2 shows internal resistance; all measurements are organized by temperature.
items.explanation: At 20°C, 30°C, and 40°C, capacity exceeds 900 mAh and resistance is below 0.50 ohm. The 10°C battery fails both requirements.

per_choice.correct: At 20°C, 30°C, and 40°C, capacity exceeds 900 mAh and resistance is below 0.50 ohm. The 10°C battery fails both requirements.
per_choice.trap: A student may choose only 30°C because it has the best capacity and lowest resistance, rather than including every temperature that meets both thresholds.

5–10 min

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, which statement correctly compares the cooling of the two containers during the first and second 10-minute periods?
choices: Container A cooled more during the first 10 minutes, but Container B cooled more during the second 10 minutes.
Both containers cooled more during the first 10 minutes, and Container A's difference between the periods was greater.
Both containers cooled more during the second 10 minutes, and Container B's difference between the periods was greater.
Both containers cooled by the same amount during the first and second 10-minute periods.
items.stimulus: A student measured the temperature of water as it cooled in two containers over 20 minutes. Container A was uncovered, while Container B was covered during the measurements. Table 1 lists the measurements for Container A, Figure 1 graphs the measurements for Container B, and Figure 2 graphs measurements for both containers.
items.explanation: Container A cooled 22°C from 0–10 minutes and 14°C from 10–20 minutes. Container B cooled 13°C and 9°C during those periods, respectively. Thus both cooled more at first, and A's difference was larger.

per_choice.correct: Container A cooled 22°C from 0–10 minutes and 14°C from 10–20 minutes. Container B cooled 13°C and 9°C during those periods, respectively. Thus both cooled more at first, and A's difference was larger.
per_choice.trap: A student may compare only the final temperatures or may reverse the two 10-minute periods.

items.tests: Recognising which graph represents a given table, or the reverse.

items.stem: Which series in Figure 2 represents the data in Table 1?
choices: Container B
The series that begins at 68°C
The series that ends at 58°C
Container A
items.stimulus: A student measured the temperature of water as it cooled in two containers over 20 minutes. Container A was uncovered, while Container B was covered during the measurements. Table 1 lists the measurements for Container A, Figure 1 graphs the measurements for Container B, and Figure 2 graphs measurements for both containers.
items.explanation: Table 1 begins at 80°C and has values of 68°C, 58°C, 50°C, and 44°C at 5-minute intervals. These points match the Container A series in Figure 2.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 begins at 80°C and has values of 68°C, 58°C, 50°C, and 44°C at 5-minute intervals. These points match the Container A series in Figure 2.
per_choice.trap: A student may select Container B because both series begin at 80°C, or choose the ending value from the wrong series.

items.tests: Recognising which graph represents a given table, or the reverse.

items.stem: According to Table 1, approximately what percentage of Container A's total temperature decrease by 20 minutes had occurred by 15 minutes?
items.stimulus: A student measured the temperature of water as it cooled in two containers over 20 minutes. Container A was uncovered, while Container B was covered during the measurements. Table 1 lists the measurements for Container A, Figure 1 graphs the measurements for Container B, and Figure 2 graphs measurements for both containers.
items.explanation: The total decrease was 80 − 44 = 36°C. By 15 minutes, the decrease was 80 − 50 = 30°C. The fraction is 30/36, or approximately 83%.

per_choice.correct: The total decrease was 80 − 44 = 36°C. By 15 minutes, the decrease was 80 − 50 = 30°C. The fraction is 30/36, or approximately 83%.
per_choice.trap: A student may divide the 15-minute temperature, 50, by the starting temperature, or use the decrease during only the final 5 minutes.

Table 1 shows initial and final concentrations, Figure 1 shows concentration over time, and Figure 2 shows the volume of water processed during the trial. The filter setup names are used in all three displays.

items.stimulus: Researchers tested how four filter setups removed blue dye from water. Each setup received the same starting dye concentration, and dye concentration was measured during a 10-minute trial. items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 2, which setup removed the greatest total mass of dye during the 10-minute trial? Assume mass removed equals concentration decrease multiplied by the volume processed in liters.
choices: Sand + carbon
Activated carbon
No filter
Sand
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how four filter setups removed blue dye from water. Each setup received the same starting dye concentration, and dye concentration was measured during a 10-minute trial. Table 1 shows initial and final concentrations, Figure 1 shows concentration over time, and Figure 2 shows the volume of water processed during the trial. The filter setup names are used in all three displays.
items.explanation: Sand removed 10 mg/L × 0.080 L = 0.80 mg. Sand + carbon removed 32 mg/L × 0.040 L = 1.28 mg. Activated carbon removed 24 mg/L × 0.060 L = 1.44 mg, the greatest amount. No filter removed none.

per_choice.correct: Sand removed 10 mg/L × 0.080 L = 0.80 mg. Sand + carbon removed 32 mg/L × 0.040 L = 1.28 mg. Activated carbon removed 24 mg/L × 0.060 L = 1.44 mg, the greatest amount. No filter removed none.
per_choice.trap: Sand + carbon has the largest concentration decrease in Table 1, but it processed the smallest volume in Figure 2.

items.stem: What was the average dye concentration for the activated-carbon setup at 5 minutes and 10 minutes, according to Figure 1?
choices: 16 mg/L
24 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how four filter setups removed blue dye from water. Each setup received the same starting dye concentration, and dye concentration was measured during a 10-minute trial. Table 1 shows initial and final concentrations, Figure 1 shows concentration over time, and Figure 2 shows the volume of water processed during the trial. The filter setup names are used in all three displays.
items.explanation: Figure 1 gives 21 mg/L at 5 minutes and 16 mg/L at 10 minutes. Their average is (21 + 16) ÷ 2 = 18.5 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 gives 21 mg/L at 5 minutes and 16 mg/L at 10 minutes. Their average is (21 + 16) ÷ 2 = 18.5 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: 16 mg/L is only the 10-minute value; 20.5 mg/L comes from averaging the 5-minute value with the initial 40 mg/L value.

items.tests: A difference, ratio, rate or average computed from displayed values.

items.stem: According to Table 1, the pressure at 25 mL was how many times the pressure at 50 mL?
choices: 0.5 times
1 time
2 times
4 times
items.stimulus: Researchers compressed the same amount of air in a sealed syringe to several target volumes while keeping the temperature constant. At each volume, they measured the air pressure, the force needed to hold the piston in place, and the time required for the pressure reading to stabilize. Table 1 shows pressure measurements, Figure 1 shows holding force measurements, and Figure 2 shows stabilization times for the same target volumes.
items.explanation: The pressure was 200 kPa at 25 mL and 100 kPa at 50 mL. Because 200 ÷ 100 = 2, the pressure at 25 mL was 2 times as great.

per_choice.correct: The pressure was 200 kPa at 25 mL and 100 kPa at 50 mL. Because 200 ÷ 100 = 2, the pressure at 25 mL was 2 times as great.
per_choice.trap: A student may reverse the comparison and calculate 100 ÷ 200, obtaining 0.5.

items.tests: Whether two quantities vary directly, inversely, or not at all.

items.stem: At which volume were both the pressure in Table 1 and the holding force in Figure 1 one-half of their respective values at 20 mL?
choices: 25 mL
40 mL
50 mL
80 mL
items.stimulus: Researchers compressed the same amount of air in a sealed syringe to several target volumes while keeping the temperature constant. At each volume, they measured the air pressure, the force needed to hold the piston in place, and the time required for the pressure reading to stabilize. Table 1 shows pressure measurements, Figure 1 shows holding force measurements, and Figure 2 shows stabilization times for the same target volumes.
items.explanation: At 20 mL, the pressure was 250 kPa and the force was 50 N. Half of these values are 125 kPa and 25 N, which occur together at 40 mL.

per_choice.correct: At 20 mL, the pressure was 250 kPa and the force was 50 N. Half of these values are 125 kPa and 25 N, which occur together at 40 mL.
per_choice.trap: A student may select 50 mL by noticing that its pressure is close to half of 250 kPa but failing to check the force in Figure 1.

items.stem: When the volume increased from 40 mL to 80 mL, what happened to the pressure and holding force?
choices: Both decreased by 50%.
Both decreased by 75%.
The pressure decreased by 75%, but the force decreased by 50%.
The pressure decreased by 50%, but the force decreased by 25%.
items.stimulus: Researchers compressed the same amount of air in a sealed syringe to several target volumes while keeping the temperature constant. At each volume, they measured the air pressure, the force needed to hold the piston in place, and the time required for the pressure reading to stabilize. Table 1 shows pressure measurements, Figure 1 shows holding force measurements, and Figure 2 shows stabilization times for the same target volumes.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows pressure decreasing from 125 to 62.5 kPa, a 50% decrease. Figure 1 shows force decreasing from 25 to 12.5 N, also a 50% decrease.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows pressure decreasing from 125 to 62.5 kPa, a 50% decrease. Figure 1 shows force decreasing from 25 to 12.5 N, also a 50% decrease.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between target volume and stabilization time in Figure 2?
choices: The time varies inversely with volume.
The time increases only when volume exceeds 50 mL.
The time varies directly with volume.
The time does not vary systematically with volume.
items.stimulus: Researchers compressed the same amount of air in a sealed syringe to several target volumes while keeping the temperature constant. At each volume, they measured the air pressure, the force needed to hold the piston in place, and the time required for the pressure reading to stabilize. Table 1 shows pressure measurements, Figure 1 shows holding force measurements, and Figure 2 shows stabilization times for the same target volumes.
items.explanation: The stabilization time is 8 s at every tested volume, so it remains constant rather than increasing or decreasing as volume changes.

per_choice.correct: The stabilization time is 8 s at every tested volume, so it remains constant rather than increasing or decreasing as volume changes.
per_choice.trap: A student may infer an inverse relationship from the pressure data in Table 1 and incorrectly apply it to the separate time measurements.

items.tests: Whether two quantities vary directly, inversely, or not at all.

items.stem: Which statement correctly identifies the variables in Experiment 1, using Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: Seeds per dish were varied, and root length was measured.
Germination percentage was varied, and nitrate concentration was measured.
Days were varied, and nitrate concentration was measured.
Nitrate concentration was varied, and germination percentage was measured.
items.stimulus: Researchers conducted two experiments using the same type of seed. In Experiment 1, dishes received different nitrate concentrations, and the percentage of seeds that germinated after 7 days was recorded; in Experiment 2, average root length after 7 days was measured. Table 1 shows the nitrate concentrations and conditions used in both experiments, while Figure 1 shows the germination results and Figure 2 shows the root-length results. Each plotted value is the mean for several dishes.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows that nitrate concentration changed while days and seeds per dish stayed constant; Figure 1 reports germination percentage.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows that nitrate concentration changed while days and seeds per dish stayed constant; Figure 1 reports germination percentage.
per_choice.trap: The choice involving days or seeds per dish mistakes a controlled condition for the experimental variable, while the last choice reverses the independent and dependent variables.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Why is the effect of nitrate concentration on root length reasonably comparable across the treatments shown in Table 1 and Figure 2?
choices: The highest nitrate treatment produced the longest roots.
The number of seeds and the growth period were the same for every treatment.
Root length and germination percentage were measured in the same units.
The nitrate concentration was the same in every treatment.
items.stimulus: Researchers conducted two experiments using the same type of seed. In Experiment 1, dishes received different nitrate concentrations, and the percentage of seeds that germinated after 7 days was recorded; in Experiment 2, average root length after 7 days was measured. Table 1 shows the nitrate concentrations and conditions used in both experiments, while Figure 1 shows the germination results and Figure 2 shows the root-length results. Each plotted value is the mean for several dishes.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows 25 seeds per dish and 7 days for every nitrate level, so these factors were controlled while Figure 2 compares root lengths.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows 25 seeds per dish and 7 days for every nitrate level, so these factors were controlled while Figure 2 compares root lengths.
per_choice.trap: The highest treatment did not produce the longest roots, and equal measurement units are not required for comparing treatments within one experiment.

items.explanation: Thirty mg/L is halfway between 20 and 40 mg/L. Halfway between 83% and 79% is 81%, and halfway between 17 mm and 15 mm is 16 mm.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Which condition served as the control group, and why was it useful? Use Table 1 and Figure 1.
choices: 0 mg/L, because it provided growth and oxygen values without added copper sulfate
0.5 mg/L, because it was the lowest concentration that contained copper sulfate
1 mg/L, because it was the middle concentration tested
2 mg/L, because it produced the strongest treatment effect
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects duckweed growth in two experiments. In Experiment 1, each container began with 10 fronds in 100 mL of nutrient solution and was kept at 22°C under 12 hours of light per day; only the copper sulfate concentration varied. Experiment 2 used the same concentrations and starting conditions but measured oxygen production after 24 hours. Table 1 shows frond counts from Experiment 1, Figure 1 shows oxygen production from Experiment 2, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of fronds surviving after 5 days.
items.explanation: The 0 mg/L condition had no added copper sulfate and supplied the baseline final-frond count and oxygen production for comparison with treated groups.

per_choice.correct: The 0 mg/L condition had no added copper sulfate and supplied the baseline final-frond count and oxygen production for comparison with treated groups.
per_choice.trap: The 0.5 mg/L choice confuses the lowest treatment concentration with the no-treatment control; the 2 mg/L choice identifies the strongest treatment rather than the baseline.

items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects duckweed growth in two experiments. In Experiment 1, each container began with 10 fronds in 100 mL of nutrient solution and was kept at 22°C under 12 hours of light per day; only the copper sulfate concentration varied. Experiment 2 used the same concentrations and starting conditions but measured oxygen production after 24 hours. Table 1 shows frond counts from Experiment 1, Figure 1 shows oxygen production from Experiment 2, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of fronds surviving after 5 days.
items.explanation: The passage states that every container began with 10 fronds, so differences in final frond counts were not caused by different starting sample sizes.

items.stem: Compared with the control, approximately what percentage decrease in oxygen production occurred at 1 mg/L copper sulfate? Use Figure 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how copper sulfate concentration affects duckweed growth in two experiments. In Experiment 1, each container began with 10 fronds in 100 mL of nutrient solution and was kept at 22°C under 12 hours of light per day; only the copper sulfate concentration varied. Experiment 2 used the same concentrations and starting conditions but measured oxygen production after 24 hours. Table 1 shows frond counts from Experiment 1, Figure 1 shows oxygen production from Experiment 2, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of fronds surviving after 5 days.
items.explanation: Oxygen production decreased from 12 mL in the control to 7 mL at 1 mg/L. The decrease is 5/12, or approximately 42%.

per_choice.correct: Oxygen production decreased from 12 mL in the control to 7 mL at 1 mg/L. The decrease is 5/12, or approximately 42%.
per_choice.trap: The 25% choice treats the 5 mL decrease as a fraction of 20, and 50% rounds the decrease too far; 75% reverses the comparison with the remaining amount.

items.stem: Which pairing correctly identifies the manipulated variable and the measured variable represented by the 7-day series in Figure 1?
choices: Growth time was manipulated; NaCl concentration was measured.
NaCl concentration was manipulated; root length was measured.
Lateral-root number was manipulated; root length was measured.
Root length was manipulated; NaCl concentration was measured.
items.stimulus: Students investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of bean seedlings. Seedlings were grown for either 7 or 14 days in solutions containing the same tested concentrations, and root length and lateral-root number were recorded. Table 1 lists measurements at 7 days, Figure 1 compares root length at the two growth times, and Figure 2 shows lateral-root counts at 7 days.
items.explanation: NaCl concentration is the variable placed on the horizontal axis and changed by the researchers, while root length is the response on the vertical axis.

per_choice.correct: NaCl concentration is the variable placed on the horizontal axis and changed by the researchers, while root length is the response on the vertical axis.
per_choice.trap: The two lines may make growth time seem like the only manipulated variable, but time distinguishes the series; the concentration is the input varied along the axis.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: According to Figure 1, how much greater was the root length after 14 days than after 7 days at 50 mM NaCl?
choices: 3 cm
5 cm
7 cm
9 cm
items.stimulus: Students investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of bean seedlings. Seedlings were grown for either 7 or 14 days in solutions containing the same tested concentrations, and root length and lateral-root number were recorded. Table 1 lists measurements at 7 days, Figure 1 compares root length at the two growth times, and Figure 2 shows lateral-root counts at 7 days.
items.explanation: At 50 mM, the 14-day series is 14 cm and the 7-day series is 9 cm, so 14 - 9 = 5 cm.

per_choice.correct: At 50 mM, the 14-day series is 14 cm and the 7-day series is 9 cm, so 14 - 9 = 5 cm.
per_choice.trap: A reader may compare the two concentrations within one time series or use the 0 mM values instead of comparing the two time series at 50 mM.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, which statement correctly compares the 50 mM treatment with the 0 mM treatment at 7 days?
choices: Root length decreased by 2 cm, and lateral-root number decreased by 3.
Root length decreased by 2 cm, and lateral-root number decreased by 5.
Root length decreased by 1 cm, and lateral-root number decreased by 5.
Root length decreased by 1 cm, and lateral-root number decreased by 3.
items.stimulus: Students investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of bean seedlings. Seedlings were grown for either 7 or 14 days in solutions containing the same tested concentrations, and root length and lateral-root number were recorded. Table 1 lists measurements at 7 days, Figure 1 compares root length at the two growth times, and Figure 2 shows lateral-root counts at 7 days.
items.explanation: Figure 1 gives root lengths of 10 cm and 9 cm, a 1-cm decrease. Table 1 gives lateral-root counts of 8 and 5, a decrease of 3.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 gives root lengths of 10 cm and 9 cm, a 1-cm decrease. Table 1 gives lateral-root counts of 8 and 5, a decrease of 3.
per_choice.trap: The 100 mM row gives the 3-cm root-length decrease and 5-root decrease, so using that row produces a tempting but incorrect pair.

items.trap: The 100 mM row gives the 3-cm root-length decrease and 5-root decrease, so using that row produces a tempting but incorrect pair.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: Suppose a follow-up study kept NaCl concentration at 50 mM but varied exposure time using the two times shown in Figure 1. Which statement correctly identifies the newly manipulated variable and the measured variable?
choices: Root length would be manipulated, and exposure time would be measured.
Lateral-root number would be manipulated, and exposure time would be measured.
Exposure time would be manipulated, and root length would be measured.
NaCl concentration would be manipulated, and lateral-root number would be measured.
items.stimulus: Students investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of bean seedlings. Seedlings were grown for either 7 or 14 days in solutions containing the same tested concentrations, and root length and lateral-root number were recorded. Table 1 lists measurements at 7 days, Figure 1 compares root length at the two growth times, and Figure 2 shows lateral-root counts at 7 days.
items.explanation: The follow-up would change the 7-day versus 14-day condition, making exposure time the manipulated variable; root length remains the response read on Figure 1's vertical axis.

per_choice.correct: The follow-up would change the 7-day versus 14-day condition, making exposure time the manipulated variable; root length remains the response read on Figure 1's vertical axis.
per_choice.trap: The concentration is the original manipulated variable, but the proposed follow-up holds it constant and instead changes time.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: Why was a dark flask tested at each temperature, as shown by the measurements in Table 1?
choices: To determine whether the lamp became brighter at higher temperatures
To determine how much oxygen change was caused by respiration rather than photosynthesis
To make the plant produce oxygen at the same rate at all temperatures
To measure the oxygen concentration at the beginning of the light experiment only
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how water temperature affected the rate at which an aquatic plant produced oxygen. Identical plant samples were placed in sealed flasks at 15°C, 25°C, or 35°C, with the light flasks exposed to the same lamp. At each temperature, a dark flask was also tested to measure oxygen change without photosynthesis. Table 1 gives oxygen-change rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen concentration over time in the light flasks, and Figure 2 shows net oxygen-production rates calculated from the light and dark measurements.
items.explanation: The dark rates show oxygen decrease when photosynthesis cannot occur, so they estimate respiration and allow the light measurements to be corrected for it.

per_choice.correct: The dark rates show oxygen decrease when photosynthesis cannot occur, so they estimate respiration and allow the light measurements to be corrected for it.
per_choice.trap: Choice C confuses a control measurement with a way to equalize the results; choice D uses a starting measurement not represented by the dark rates; choice A refers to lamp brightness, which was not measured.

items.tests: Why a particular procedure or measurement was included.

items.stem: Which temperature produced the greatest oxygen increase during the 15-minute light trial in Figure 1, and is that conclusion consistent with Figure 2?
choices: 15°C; yes
25°C; yes
35°C; yes
35°C; no
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how water temperature affected the rate at which an aquatic plant produced oxygen. Identical plant samples were placed in sealed flasks at 15°C, 25°C, or 35°C, with the light flasks exposed to the same lamp. At each temperature, a dark flask was also tested to measure oxygen change without photosynthesis. Table 1 gives oxygen-change rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen concentration over time in the light flasks, and Figure 2 shows net oxygen-production rates calculated from the light and dark measurements.
items.explanation: In Figure 1, the 25°C series rises from 6 mg to 18 mg, the largest increase. Figure 2 also shows the greatest net rate at 25°C.

per_choice.correct: In Figure 1, the 25°C series rises from 6 mg to 18 mg, the largest increase. Figure 2 also shows the greatest net rate at 25°C.
per_choice.trap: The 15°C and 35°C lines both increase by only 6 mg; choosing 35°C may result from focusing on its initial rise or from reading the wrong temperature bar.

items.tests: Why a particular procedure or measurement was included.

items.stem: Net oxygen-production rate was calculated as the light rate plus the dark rate. Using Table 1, what was the net rate at 25°C, and does Figure 2 show the same value approximately?
choices: 0.10 mg/min; no
0.70 mg/min; yes
0.80 mg/min; no
0.90 mg/min; yes
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how water temperature affected the rate at which an aquatic plant produced oxygen. Identical plant samples were placed in sealed flasks at 15°C, 25°C, or 35°C, with the light flasks exposed to the same lamp. At each temperature, a dark flask was also tested to measure oxygen change without photosynthesis. Table 1 gives oxygen-change rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen concentration over time in the light flasks, and Figure 2 shows net oxygen-production rates calculated from the light and dark measurements.
items.explanation: At 25°C, 0.80 mg/min + (-0.10 mg/min) = 0.70 mg/min. Figure 2 gives approximately 0.70 mg/min for 25°C.

per_choice.correct: At 25°C, 0.80 mg/min + (-0.10 mg/min) = 0.70 mg/min. Figure 2 gives approximately 0.70 mg/min for 25°C.
per_choice.trap: 0.80 mg/min ignores respiration, 0.90 mg/min subtracts the negative dark value incorrectly, and 0.10 mg/min uses only the magnitude of the dark rate.

items.tests: Why a particular procedure or measurement was included.

items.stem: Why did the researchers record oxygen concentration every 5 minutes, rather than only recording it at the end of the trial?
choices: To measure respiration without using the dark flasks
To ensure that the final oxygen concentration was identical at all temperatures
To determine the rate over time and detect whether oxygen production began to level off
To identify which flask contained the largest plant sample
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how water temperature affected the rate at which an aquatic plant produced oxygen. Identical plant samples were placed in sealed flasks at 15°C, 25°C, or 35°C, with the light flasks exposed to the same lamp. At each temperature, a dark flask was also tested to measure oxygen change without photosynthesis. Table 1 gives oxygen-change rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen concentration over time in the light flasks, and Figure 2 shows net oxygen-production rates calculated from the light and dark measurements.
items.explanation: The repeated measurements in Figure 1 allow the researchers to compare slopes and notice that the 35°C series begins to level off after 10 minutes.

per_choice.correct: The repeated measurements in Figure 1 allow the researchers to compare slopes and notice that the 35°C series begins to level off after 10 minutes.
per_choice.trap: The final concentrations are not identical, and respiration was measured with dark flasks; plant size was controlled rather than identified from the oxygen readings.

items.stem: According to Table 1 and Figure 2, at which temperature did the carbon dioxide volume increase from the preceding temperature while the percentage of viable cells decreased?
items.stimulus: Researchers tested how temperature affected fermentation by placing equal amounts of baker's yeast and glucose solution in sealed flasks for 5 minutes. The temperature was the variable changed among trials, while the glucose amount and flask volume were held constant. Table 1 shows carbon dioxide collected after 5 minutes, Figure 1 shows the corresponding average carbon dioxide production rate, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of yeast cells remaining viable. A further trial at a temperature not used in the experiment can be predicted from the patterns in the displays.
items.explanation: From 30 C to 40 C, carbon dioxide increased from 31 mL to 38 mL, while viable cells decreased from 98% to 82%.

per_choice.correct: From 30 C to 40 C, carbon dioxide increased from 31 mL to 38 mL, while viable cells decreased from 98% to 82%.
per_choice.trap: Choosing 50 C notices that viability decreased but overlooks that carbon dioxide volume also decreased.
