items.stem: A researcher claims that insulation did not affect cooling because both beakers began at the same temperature. Which evaluation is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: The claim is supported because equal starting temperatures make all later temperatures equivalent.
The claim is supported because Beaker A and Beaker B had equal temperatures at 20 min.
The claim is not supported because after the equal starting point, Beaker A remained warmer than Beaker B at every later recorded time.
The claim is not supported because Beaker B began colder and therefore had more time to cool.
items.stimulus: A student investigated whether insulation changes how quickly 100 mL of water cools from an initial temperature of 80°C. Beaker A was placed inside an insulated sleeve, while identical Beaker B remained exposed; temperature probes recorded both beakers at 5-minute intervals in the same room. Table 1 lists the recorded temperatures, and Figure 1 plots those same measurements against time. Figure 2 shows the paired-beaker apparatus used for the investigation.
items.explanation: The displays show equal initial temperatures, but the later points are different: A is warmer than B at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min. Thus the equal starting point does not support the claim that insulation had no effect.

per_choice.correct: The displays show equal initial temperatures, but the later points are different: A is warmer than B at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min. Thus the equal starting point does not support the claim that insulation had no effect.
per_choice.trap: The first choice incorrectly treats one equal starting value as proof of equal later values; the second reverses the endpoints, and the fourth contradicts the 0-min row.

items.tests: Recognising which graph represents a given table, or the reverse.

items.stem: In Experiment 1, which variable was deliberately manipulated, rather than merely changing as a consequence of the manipulation? Use the procedure and Table 1.
choices: Distance between the lamp and flask
Irradiance reaching the flask
Temperature of the algae suspension
Oxygen concentration after 10 minutes
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how light conditions affected oxygen production by green algae. In Experiment 1, the distance between an LED lamp and an algae flask was varied while temperature was held at 25°C; Table 1 shows the lamp distance, irradiance, and oxygen concentration after 10 minutes. In Experiment 2, oxygen concentration was measured at several lamp distances and temperatures; Figure 1 shows those oxygen measurements. The same 100 mL algae suspension and exposure time were used in every run, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to deliver light and measure oxygen.
items.explanation: The procedure says distance was varied in Experiment 1. Table 1 shows that irradiance and oxygen changed with distance, so they were responses or associated measurements rather than the selected manipulation.

per_choice.correct: The procedure says distance was varied in Experiment 1. Table 1 shows that irradiance and oxygen changed with distance, so they were responses or associated measurements rather than the selected manipulation.
per_choice.trap: Choosing irradiance confuses a measured light condition with the distance that the researchers directly adjusted.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: Which quantity was the measured response in both experiments, as indicated by the apparatus and the vertical axis of Figure 1?
choices: Distance from lamp to flask
Irradiance at the flask
Temperature of the suspension
Oxygen concentration
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how light conditions affected oxygen production by green algae. In Experiment 1, the distance between an LED lamp and an algae flask was varied while temperature was held at 25°C; Table 1 shows the lamp distance, irradiance, and oxygen concentration after 10 minutes. In Experiment 2, oxygen concentration was measured at several lamp distances and temperatures; Figure 1 shows those oxygen measurements. The same 100 mL algae suspension and exposure time were used in every run, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to deliver light and measure oxygen.
items.explanation: Figure 2 identifies an O2 sensor, and Figure 1 labels its vertical axis Oxygen (mg/L). Distance and temperature were experimental conditions, not the sensor's response.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: The 25°C series in Figure 1 matches Experiment 1. From 10 cm to 40 cm, what was the approximate percentage decrease in oxygen concentration? Use Table 1 to identify the two corresponding measurements.
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how light conditions affected oxygen production by green algae. In Experiment 1, the distance between an LED lamp and an algae flask was varied while temperature was held at 25°C; Table 1 shows the lamp distance, irradiance, and oxygen concentration after 10 minutes. In Experiment 2, oxygen concentration was measured at several lamp distances and temperatures; Figure 1 shows those oxygen measurements. The same 100 mL algae suspension and exposure time were used in every run, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to deliver light and measure oxygen.
items.explanation: At 10 cm, oxygen was 18 mg/L, and at 40 cm it was 7 mg/L. The decrease was 11 mg/L; 11 divided by 18 is about 61.1%.

items.stimulus: Researchers studied how light conditions affected oxygen production by green algae. In Experiment 1, the distance between an LED lamp and an algae flask was varied while temperature was held at 25°C; Table 1 shows the lamp distance, irradiance, and oxygen concentration after 10 minutes. In Experiment 2, oxygen concentration was measured at several lamp distances and temperatures; Figure 1 shows those oxygen measurements. The same 100 mL algae suspension and exposure time were used in every run, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to deliver light and measure oxygen.

items.stem: Why was the 10-minute exposure time, stated in the passage, an important control when the oxygen values in Table 1 were compared?
choices: It allowed oxygen amounts to be compared after the same accumulation period
It made the lamp distance equal to the irradiance value
It converted the temperature series into a single temperature
It caused the sensor to measure distance instead of oxygen
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how light conditions affected oxygen production by green algae. In Experiment 1, the distance between an LED lamp and an algae flask was varied while temperature was held at 25°C; Table 1 shows the lamp distance, irradiance, and oxygen concentration after 10 minutes. In Experiment 2, oxygen concentration was measured at several lamp distances and temperatures; Figure 1 shows those oxygen measurements. The same 100 mL algae suspension and exposure time were used in every run, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to deliver light and measure oxygen.
items.explanation: Because oxygen was allowed to accumulate for the same 10 minutes in every run, differences in the final oxygen readings could be compared without different elapsed times being an additional factor.

per_choice.correct: Because oxygen was allowed to accumulate for the same 10 minutes in every run, differences in the final oxygen readings could be compared without different elapsed times being an additional factor.
per_choice.trap: The other choices substitute a plotted or measured variable for the purpose of controlling elapsed time.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: A researcher hypothesized that increasing irradiance increases algal oxygen production, regardless of temperature. Which observation from both displays most directly supports this hypothesis?
choices: As distance increased, irradiance and oxygen both decreased, and the same oxygen direction appeared for all three temperature series
The 35°C series had the highest oxygen value at every distance, while Table 1 listed only one temperature
The oxygen sensor was positioned after the algae flask, and Table 1 included five trials
The 25°C values in Figure 1 matched the oxygen column in Table 1, while temperature was varied in Experiment 2
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how light conditions affected oxygen production by green algae. In Experiment 1, the distance between an LED lamp and an algae flask was varied while temperature was held at 25°C; Table 1 shows the lamp distance, irradiance, and oxygen concentration after 10 minutes. In Experiment 2, oxygen concentration was measured at several lamp distances and temperatures; Figure 1 shows those oxygen measurements. The same 100 mL algae suspension and exposure time were used in every run, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to deliver light and measure oxygen.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows irradiance decreasing as distance increases, while oxygen also decreases. Figure 1 shows the same distance-related oxygen trend at 15°C, 25°C, and 35°C, supporting the stated relationship across temperatures.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows irradiance decreasing as distance increases, while oxygen also decreases. Figure 1 shows the same distance-related oxygen trend at 15°C, 25°C, and 35°C, supporting the stated relationship across temperatures.
per_choice.trap: The second choice supports a temperature effect, and the last choice confirms consistency between displays but does not itself support the irradiance hypothesis.

items.tests: Telling the manipulated variable from the measured one.

items.stem: A new experiment indicates that plants remove 25% of the nitrate present at the 30-cm port before the sample is analyzed. Under slow flow, what concentration would the analysis report if this plant uptake occurred?
choices: 8 mg/L
9 mg/L
10 mg/L
15 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how nitrate moves through a layered soil column when water enters at either a slow or a fast flow rate. A nitrate solution initially containing 20 mg/L nitrate was introduced at the surface, and samples were collected from ports at several depths after 24 hours. Table 1 shows nitrate concentrations for the two flow rates, Figure 1 shows dissolved oxygen at the same depths, and Figure 2 shows the soil layers and locations of the sampling ports. The researchers used the results to evaluate a model in which nitrate removal depends on both movement through the layers and microbial activity.
items.explanation: Table 1 gives 12 mg/L at 30 cm under slow flow. Removing 25% leaves 75%: 0.75 × 12 = 9 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 gives 12 mg/L at 30 cm under slow flow. Removing 25% leaves 75%: 0.75 × 12 = 9 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: The 8 mg/L choice is the measured slow-flow value at 70 cm, 10 mg/L results from an incorrect one-third reduction, and 15 mg/L is the fast-flow value at 30 cm.

choices: 0.2 mg/L O2 and 1 mg/L biomass
0.5 mg/L O2 and 1 mg/L biomass
0.5 mg/L O2 and 5 mg/L biomass
1.0 mg/L O2 and 0.5 mg/L biomass
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. Figure 2 represents the proposed sequence by which nitrate availability could affect dissolved oxygen.
items.explanation: In the high-light series, net oxygen change rises from 10.0 to 10.5 mg/L, a change of 0.5 mg/L. Table 1 shows biomass rising from 30 to 31 mg/L, a change of 1 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: In the high-light series, net oxygen change rises from 10.0 to 10.5 mg/L, a change of 0.5 mg/L. Table 1 shows biomass rising from 30 to 31 mg/L, a change of 1 mg/L.

items.stem: Which initial nitrate concentration most strongly indicates that additional nitrate had become excess rather than limiting under high light, based on both Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: 0 mg/L
2 mg/L
5 mg/L
10 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. Figure 2 represents the proposed sequence by which nitrate availability could affect dissolved oxygen.
items.explanation: At 10 mg/L, Table 1 shows substantial nitrate remaining and only a 1 mg/L biomass increase over the 5 mg/L treatment. Figure 1 likewise shows the high-light oxygen value nearly leveling off from 5 to 10 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: At 10 mg/L, Table 1 shows substantial nitrate remaining and only a 1 mg/L biomass increase over the 5 mg/L treatment. Figure 1 likewise shows the high-light oxygen value nearly leveling off from 5 to 10 mg/L.

items.stem: The researchers want to test whether the near-plateau in the high-light series from 5 to 10 mg/L reflects nitrate saturation rather than a measurement ceiling. Which additional treatment would provide the strongest test, using the relationships shown in Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: A nitrate-free culture under high light with no algae, measuring only the water's oxygen concentration
A 15 mg/L nitrate culture under high light, with final nitrate, biomass, and oxygen measured in the same ways
A 15 mg/L nitrate culture under low light, with only oxygen measured
A 10 mg/L nitrate culture under high light with twice the light intensity, with no biomass measurement
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. Figure 2 represents the proposed sequence by which nitrate availability could affect dissolved oxygen.
items.explanation: A higher-nitrate, high-light treatment extends the same comparison while measuring both the intermediate biomass and the final oxygen response. If oxygen and biomass remain near the 5-to-10 mg/L values, saturation is supported; if they rise, the apparent plateau may have reflected the tested range.

per_choice.correct: A higher-nitrate, high-light treatment extends the same comparison while measuring both the intermediate biomass and the final oxygen response. If oxygen and biomass remain near the 5-to-10 mg/L values, saturation is supported; if they rise, the apparent plateau may have reflected the tested range.
per_choice.trap: Choice C changes light while extending nitrate, so it cannot isolate saturation; choice D changes light and omits the pathway intermediate; choice A removes the algal pathway rather than testing the plateau.

items.stem: Assuming each high-light series segment in Figure 1 is linear, what pair of values would be estimated at an initial nitrate concentration of 7.5 mg/L for net oxygen change and algal biomass, respectively, using Figure 1 and Table 1?
choices: 5.25 mg/L O2 and 30.0 mg/L biomass
10.25 mg/L O2 and 30.5 mg/L biomass
10.50 mg/L O2 and 31.0 mg/L biomass
15.00 mg/L O2 and 35.0 mg/L biomass
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. Figure 2 represents the proposed sequence by which nitrate availability could affect dissolved oxygen.
items.explanation: A value of 7.5 mg/L is halfway between 5 and 10 mg/L. Figure 1 gives halfway between 10.0 and 10.5 as 10.25 mg/L O2; Table 1 gives halfway between 30 and 31 as 30.5 mg/L biomass.

per_choice.correct: A value of 7.5 mg/L is halfway between 5 and 10 mg/L. Figure 1 gives halfway between 10.0 and 10.5 as 10.25 mg/L O2; Table 1 gives halfway between 30 and 31 as 30.5 mg/L biomass.
per_choice.trap: Choice A uses the wrong oxygen segment; choice C uses the 10 mg/L endpoint rather than interpolating; choice D extrapolates the early steep increase instead of using the 5-to-10 interval.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: At the 35-cm sampling depth, which combination correctly identifies the soil layer and the difference between the high-flow and low-flow nitrate concentrations, according to Table 1 and Figure 2?
choices: Sand; 9 mg/L
Clay; 23 mg/L
Clay; 9 mg/L
Sand; 23 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers applied the same nitrate fertilizer to soil columns and irrigated separate columns under low-flow or high-flow conditions. After 24 h, they measured nitrate concentration in pore water at several depths; Table 1 gives those concentrations. Figure 1 shows hydraulic conductivity at the same depths, which was used as an indicator of the rate of downward water movement. Figure 2 shows the soil layers and their depth ranges; the clay layer was expected to impede downward movement relative to sand.
items.explanation: Figure 2 places 35 cm in the sand layer. Table 1 gives 51 mg/L for high flow and 28 mg/L for low flow, a difference of 23 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 places 35 cm in the sand layer. Table 1 gives 51 mg/L for high flow and 28 mg/L for low flow, a difference of 23 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: A student may identify 35 cm as clay by using the adjacent upper layer, or subtract the 20-cm values instead of the 35-cm values.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: At 20 cm, by approximately what percentage was the high-flow nitrate concentration greater than the low-flow concentration, and in which layer was this comparison made? Use Table 1 and Figure 2.
choices: 10%; topsoil
20%; clay
25%; clay
40%; sand
items.stimulus: Researchers applied the same nitrate fertilizer to soil columns and irrigated separate columns under low-flow or high-flow conditions. After 24 h, they measured nitrate concentration in pore water at several depths; Table 1 gives those concentrations. Figure 1 shows hydraulic conductivity at the same depths, which was used as an indicator of the rate of downward water movement. Figure 2 shows the soil layers and their depth ranges; the clay layer was expected to impede downward movement relative to sand.
items.explanation: At 20 cm, the concentrations were 45 mg/L and 36 mg/L. The increase was 9/36, or 25%. Figure 2 places 20 cm in clay.

per_choice.correct: At 20 cm, the concentrations were 45 mg/L and 36 mg/L. The increase was 9/36, or 25%. Figure 2 places 20 cm in clay.
per_choice.trap: Using 9/45 gives 20%, while using the 35-cm values gives a larger difference and places the sample in sand.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: A sample collected halfway between 20 cm and 35 cm would lie in which layer, and what high-flow hydraulic conductivity would be estimated from Figure 1 at that depth?
choices: Clay; 1.3 cm/h
Sand; 1.5 cm/h
Clay; 1.7 cm/h
Sand; 1.9 cm/h
items.stimulus: Researchers applied the same nitrate fertilizer to soil columns and irrigated separate columns under low-flow or high-flow conditions. After 24 h, they measured nitrate concentration in pore water at several depths; Table 1 gives those concentrations. Figure 1 shows hydraulic conductivity at the same depths, which was used as an indicator of the rate of downward water movement. Figure 2 shows the soil layers and their depth ranges; the clay layer was expected to impede downward movement relative to sand.
items.explanation: Halfway between 20 and 35 cm is 27.5 cm, which is within the clay layer in Figure 2. The high-flow conductivity halfway between 1.8 and 1.6 cm/h is approximately 1.7 cm/h.

per_choice.correct: Halfway between 20 and 35 cm is 27.5 cm, which is within the clay layer in Figure 2. The high-flow conductivity halfway between 1.8 and 1.6 cm/h is approximately 1.7 cm/h.
per_choice.trap: A student may classify 27.5 cm as sand by rounding the depth to 30 cm, or use the low-flow series instead of the high-flow series.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between water movement and nitrate distribution when the two displays are considered together?
choices: The low-flow column had greater conductivity below the clay layer, causing its nitrate concentration to increase in the sand.
The high-flow column had greater conductivity at every measured depth, but its nitrate concentration was lower near the surface and higher at the deeper sampling depths.
The high-flow column had lower conductivity at every measured depth, and its nitrate concentration was lower at every depth.
Both columns had the same conductivity in the clay, and the nitrate difference occurred only in the topsoil.
items.stimulus: Researchers applied the same nitrate fertilizer to soil columns and irrigated separate columns under low-flow or high-flow conditions. After 24 h, they measured nitrate concentration in pore water at several depths; Table 1 gives those concentrations. Figure 1 shows hydraulic conductivity at the same depths, which was used as an indicator of the rate of downward water movement. Figure 2 shows the soil layers and their depth ranges; the clay layer was expected to impede downward movement relative to sand.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows higher conductivity for high flow at all four depths. Table 1 shows high-flow nitrate is lower at 5 cm but higher at 20, 35, and 50 cm.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows higher conductivity for high flow at all four depths. Table 1 shows high-flow nitrate is lower at 5 cm but higher at 20, 35, and 50 cm.
per_choice.trap: The distractors reverse the conductivity series, treat the low-flow nitrate values as increasing with depth, or restrict the difference to one layer.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: Suppose nitrate concentration and hydraulic conductivity both changed linearly between the measured depths. At 30 cm in the low-flow column, which pair of estimates is most reasonable? Use Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2.
choices: 19 mg/L nitrate and 0.6 cm/h conductivity
31 mg/L nitrate and 0.9 cm/h conductivity
36 mg/L nitrate and 1.0 cm/h conductivity
47 mg/L nitrate and 1.4 cm/h conductivity
items.stimulus: Researchers applied the same nitrate fertilizer to soil columns and irrigated separate columns under low-flow or high-flow conditions. After 24 h, they measured nitrate concentration in pore water at several depths; Table 1 gives those concentrations. Figure 1 shows hydraulic conductivity at the same depths, which was used as an indicator of the rate of downward water movement. Figure 2 shows the soil layers and their depth ranges; the clay layer was expected to impede downward movement relative to sand.
items.explanation: Thirty centimeters is the boundary between the clay and sand layers in Figure 2. Interpolating from 20 to 35 cm gives a low-flow nitrate concentration of about 31 mg/L and conductivity of about 0.9 cm/h.

per_choice.correct: Thirty centimeters is the boundary between the clay and sand layers in Figure 2. Interpolating from 20 to 35 cm gives a low-flow nitrate concentration of about 31 mg/L and conductivity of about 0.9 cm/h.
per_choice.trap: The first and fourth choices copy values from 50 cm, while the third choice copies the 20-cm values rather than interpolating toward 35 cm.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: At which measured depth was the difference between high-flow and low-flow nitrate concentration greatest, and what high-flow conductivity did Figure 1 show there?
choices: 5 cm; 2.0 cm/h
20 cm; 1.8 cm/h
35 cm; 1.6 cm/h
50 cm; 1.4 cm/h
items.stimulus: Researchers applied the same nitrate fertilizer to soil columns and irrigated separate columns under low-flow or high-flow conditions. After 24 h, they measured nitrate concentration in pore water at several depths; Table 1 gives those concentrations. Figure 1 shows hydraulic conductivity at the same depths, which was used as an indicator of the rate of downward water movement. Figure 2 shows the soil layers and their depth ranges; the clay layer was expected to impede downward movement relative to sand.
items.explanation: The high-flow minus low-flow nitrate differences at 5, 20, 35, and 50 cm are -3, 9, 23, and 28 mg/L, respectively. Figure 1 gives 1.4 cm/h for high flow at 50 cm.

per_choice.correct: The high-flow minus low-flow nitrate differences at 5, 20, 35, and 50 cm are -3, 9, 23, and 28 mg/L, respectively. Figure 1 gives 1.4 cm/h for high flow at 50 cm.
per_choice.trap: A student may choose 35 cm because it has the largest high-flow nitrate concentration, rather than the largest difference between conditions.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: A new column receives high-flow irrigation, but its clay layer is replaced with sand. Based on the layer arrangement in Figure 2, the conductivity pattern in Figure 1, and the nitrate values in Table 1, which outcome is most likely compared with the original high-flow column?
choices: Nitrate at 35 cm would increase while conductivity at 50 cm would decrease because sand has lower conductivity than clay.
Nitrate at both depths would be unchanged because the fertilizer amount, rather than soil structure, controls all nitrate movement.
Nitrate at 35 cm would be more likely to exceed nitrate at 50 cm because the removed clay would further slow drainage.
Nitrate at 50 cm would be more likely to increase relative to nitrate at 35 cm because removing the slower-draining layer would allow more nitrate-bearing water to move downward.
items.stimulus: Researchers applied the same nitrate fertilizer to soil columns and irrigated separate columns under low-flow or high-flow conditions. After 24 h, they measured nitrate concentration in pore water at several depths; Table 1 gives those concentrations. Figure 1 shows hydraulic conductivity at the same depths, which was used as an indicator of the rate of downward water movement. Figure 2 shows the soil layers and their depth ranges; the clay layer was expected to impede downward movement relative to sand.
items.explanation: Figure 2 identifies clay as the slower-draining layer, while Figure 1 links faster water movement with higher conductivity. Table 1 shows nitrate is already transported to deep samples under high flow; replacing clay with sand would most likely favor still greater movement toward 50 cm relative to 35 cm.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 identifies clay as the slower-draining layer, while Figure 1 links faster water movement with higher conductivity. Table 1 shows nitrate is already transported to deep samples under high flow; replacing clay with sand would most likely favor still greater movement toward 50 cm relative to 35 cm.
per_choice.trap: The third choice reverses the effect of removing clay, the third ignores the displayed relationship between flow and nitrate distribution, and the fourth reverses the expected conductivity of sand and clay.

items.tests: Carrying a value from one display into another to answer a single question.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 2, which live-soil sample showed the greatest nitrate removal, and from which layer was it collected?
choices: 1 mg/L removed from the clay layer
3 mg/L removed from the sand layer
4 mg/L removed from the topsoil layer
6 mg/L removed from the clay layer
items.stimulus: Researchers collected soil cores from three depths in a field and used the layers shown in Figure 2 to identify each sampling location. In Experiment 1, equal amounts of nitrate were added to live and sterilized soil from each depth, and the nitrate remaining after 48 hours was measured; the initial nitrate concentration was 10 mg/L in every core. In Experiment 2, dissolved oxygen in live soil cores from the same depths was measured repeatedly during a 6-minute incubation. Because microbial respiration consumes oxygen, the researchers used oxygen consumption as a second indicator of microbial activity.
items.explanation: Nitrate removal equals 10 mg/L initially minus the amount remaining. The 20-cm live sample removed 10 - 4 = 6 mg/L, and Figure 2 identifies 20 cm as clay.

per_choice.correct: Nitrate removal equals 10 mg/L initially minus the amount remaining. The 20-cm live sample removed 10 - 4 = 6 mg/L, and Figure 2 identifies 20 cm as clay.
per_choice.trap: The 5-cm live sample removed 4 mg/L, while the 40-cm sample removed 3 mg/L; confusing remaining nitrate with removed nitrate reverses the comparison.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Which depth would be expected to show the greatest microbial activity according to both the nitrate results in Table 1 and the oxygen results in Figure 1?
choices: 5 cm, because it has the largest oxygen concentration at 6 minutes
5 cm, because it has less nitrate remaining than the 40-cm sample
20 cm, because it has the greatest nitrate removal and oxygen consumption
40 cm, because it has more nitrate remaining and oxygen is consumed most slowly
items.stimulus: Researchers collected soil cores from three depths in a field and used the layers shown in Figure 2 to identify each sampling location. In Experiment 1, equal amounts of nitrate were added to live and sterilized soil from each depth, and the nitrate remaining after 48 hours was measured; the initial nitrate concentration was 10 mg/L in every core. In Experiment 2, dissolved oxygen in live soil cores from the same depths was measured repeatedly during a 6-minute incubation. Because microbial respiration consumes oxygen, the researchers used oxygen consumption as a second indicator of microbial activity.
items.explanation: At 20 cm, live soil leaves the least nitrate, indicating the greatest nitrate removal. Its oxygen concentration also falls from 8 to 3.5 mg/L, the largest decrease in Figure 1.

per_choice.correct: At 20 cm, live soil leaves the least nitrate, indicating the greatest nitrate removal. Its oxygen concentration also falls from 8 to 3.5 mg/L, the largest decrease in Figure 1.
per_choice.trap: The 5-cm series retains the highest oxygen concentration, but high remaining oxygen means less oxygen consumption, not more microbial activity.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Why was the sterile 20-cm soil sample included in Experiment 1, and why is it the appropriate comparison rather than the live 5-cm sample?
choices: It tests whether nitrate changes can occur without microbes while keeping depth constant.
It determines whether the 20-cm sample has more soil than the 5-cm sample.
It tests whether the clay layer contains more nitrate initially than the topsoil layer.
It provides a second measurement of oxygen consumption at the depth with the fastest decline.
items.stimulus: Researchers collected soil cores from three depths in a field and used the layers shown in Figure 2 to identify each sampling location. In Experiment 1, equal amounts of nitrate were added to live and sterilized soil from each depth, and the nitrate remaining after 48 hours was measured; the initial nitrate concentration was 10 mg/L in every core. In Experiment 2, dissolved oxygen in live soil cores from the same depths was measured repeatedly during a 6-minute incubation. Because microbial respiration consumes oxygen, the researchers used oxygen consumption as a second indicator of microbial activity.
items.explanation: The sterile 20-cm sample differs from the live 20-cm sample mainly in microbial presence, while the depth remains the same. The 5-cm sample differs in both depth and microbial condition.

per_choice.correct: The sterile 20-cm sample differs from the live 20-cm sample mainly in microbial presence, while the depth remains the same. The 5-cm sample differs in both depth and microbial condition.
per_choice.trap: The 5-cm sample is a different depth, so comparing it with the 20-cm live sample would confound depth with sterilization.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Which variable was changed systematically in Experiment 2 but was not measured repeatedly during Experiment 1?
choices: The soil layer from which the core came
Soil depth
Incubation duration
Whether the soil was sterilized
items.stimulus: Researchers collected soil cores from three depths in a field and used the layers shown in Figure 2 to identify each sampling location. In Experiment 1, equal amounts of nitrate were added to live and sterilized soil from each depth, and the nitrate remaining after 48 hours was measured; the initial nitrate concentration was 10 mg/L in every core. In Experiment 2, dissolved oxygen in live soil cores from the same depths was measured repeatedly during a 6-minute incubation. Because microbial respiration consumes oxygen, the researchers used oxygen consumption as a second indicator of microbial activity.
items.explanation: Figure 1 records oxygen at several times during a 6-minute incubation. Experiment 1 reports nitrate after a single 48-hour endpoint, although it varies depth and live versus sterile condition.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 records oxygen at several times during a 6-minute incubation. Experiment 1 reports nitrate after a single 48-hour endpoint, although it varies depth and live versus sterile condition.
per_choice.trap: Depth and soil layer are the same variable used in both experiments, and sterilization is varied in Experiment 1 rather than Experiment 2.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Which hypothesis is best supported when the live-soil nitrate data in Table 1 are considered together with the oxygen trends in Figure 1 and the layer assignments in Figure 2?
choices: Microbial activity is greatest in topsoil because topsoil begins with the highest oxygen concentration.
Microbial activity is greatest in clay because the clay sample removes the most nitrate and consumes the most oxygen.
Microbial activity is independent of depth because all samples begin Experiment 2 at the same oxygen concentration.
Microbial activity is greatest in sand because sand has the most nitrate remaining after incubation.
items.stimulus: Researchers collected soil cores from three depths in a field and used the layers shown in Figure 2 to identify each sampling location. In Experiment 1, equal amounts of nitrate were added to live and sterilized soil from each depth, and the nitrate remaining after 48 hours was measured; the initial nitrate concentration was 10 mg/L in every core. In Experiment 2, dissolved oxygen in live soil cores from the same depths was measured repeatedly during a 6-minute incubation. Because microbial respiration consumes oxygen, the researchers used oxygen consumption as a second indicator of microbial activity.
items.explanation: The 20-cm sample is in clay. It has the lowest live nitrate remaining, hence the greatest nitrate removal, and the largest oxygen decrease in Figure 1.

per_choice.correct: The 20-cm sample is in clay. It has the lowest live nitrate remaining, hence the greatest nitrate removal, and the largest oxygen decrease in Figure 1.
per_choice.trap: All samples begin with 8 mg/L oxygen, but the relevant evidence is the amount consumed during incubation, not the shared starting value.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: Suppose oxygen consumption during the first 6 minutes is proportional to nitrate removal. What ratio of the 20-cm value to the 5-cm value is supported by both experiments?
items.stimulus: Researchers collected soil cores from three depths in a field and used the layers shown in Figure 2 to identify each sampling location. In Experiment 1, equal amounts of nitrate were added to live and sterilized soil from each depth, and the nitrate remaining after 48 hours was measured; the initial nitrate concentration was 10 mg/L in every core. In Experiment 2, dissolved oxygen in live soil cores from the same depths was measured repeatedly during a 6-minute incubation. Because microbial respiration consumes oxygen, the researchers used oxygen consumption as a second indicator of microbial activity.
items.explanation: From Table 1, live nitrate removal is 6 mg/L at 20 cm and 4 mg/L at 5 cm, giving a ratio of 1.5. From Figure 1, oxygen consumption is 4.5 mg/L at 20 cm and 3 mg/L at 5 cm, also giving 1.5.

per_choice.correct: From Table 1, live nitrate removal is 6 mg/L at 20 cm and 4 mg/L at 5 cm, giving a ratio of 1.5. From Figure 1, oxygen consumption is 4.5 mg/L at 20 cm and 3 mg/L at 5 cm, also giving 1.5.
per_choice.trap: Using oxygen remaining rather than oxygen consumed gives 3.5/5, and using nitrate remaining rather than nitrate removed gives 4/6; both reverse the intended measurement.

items.tests: What was varied, what was measured, and how the studies differ.

items.stem: The researchers define the average production rate during the first 4 minutes as product formed divided by elapsed time. Using Table 1 to identify the 40 C trial and Figure 1, what was the average rate for that trial during the first 4 minutes?
choices: 6.25 units/min
7.25 units/min
8.50 units/min
10.25 units/min
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how incubation temperature affected an enzyme that converts a substrate into a colored product. In each trial, the same amounts of enzyme and substrate were mixed, incubated at a selected temperature, and sampled over time. Table 1 lists the trial temperatures and the product measured after 8 minutes, while Figure 1 shows product accumulation during the incubation. Figure 2 summarizes the repeated procedure used for each temperature trial.
items.explanation: Table 1 identifies Trial D as the 40 C trial. Figure 1 shows about 29 units at 4 minutes, so 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 units/min.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 identifies Trial D as the 40 C trial. Figure 1 shows about 29 units at 4 minutes, so 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 units/min.

items.tests: Predicting the result of a trial that was not run, from the pattern that was.

items.stem: If a trial at 35 C had been run under the same conditions, which product amount would be the best prediction for the amount measured after 8 minutes, based on Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: 39 units
44 units
47 units
53 units
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how incubation temperature affected an enzyme that converts a substrate into a colored product. In each trial, the same amounts of enzyme and substrate were mixed, incubated at a selected temperature, and sampled over time. Table 1 lists the trial temperatures and the product measured after 8 minutes, while Figure 1 shows product accumulation during the incubation. Figure 2 summarizes the repeated procedure used for each temperature trial.
items.explanation: At 8 minutes, the 30 C and 40 C trials produced 43 and 51 units, respectively. A 35 C trial lies halfway between those temperatures, and the graph shows the same increasing pattern, so approximately 47 units is the best prediction.

per_choice.correct: At 8 minutes, the 30 C and 40 C trials produced 43 and 51 units, respectively. A 35 C trial lies halfway between those temperatures, and the graph shows the same increasing pattern, so approximately 47 units is the best prediction.
per_choice.trap: 39 comes from using an earlier graph value, 53 extends the 40-to-50 trend in the wrong direction, and 44 is too close to the 30 C endpoint rather than halfway between the neighboring trials.

items.stem: Suppose the container labeled Trial D was accidentally incubated at 30 C instead of the temperature shown in Table 1. Which result would most likely have been recorded after 8 minutes, according to both displays?

39 units

items.stimulus: Researchers studied how incubation temperature affected an enzyme that converts a substrate into a colored product. In each trial, the same amounts of enzyme and substrate were mixed, incubated at a selected temperature, and sampled over time. Table 1 lists the trial temperatures and the product measured after 8 minutes, while Figure 1 shows product accumulation during the incubation. Figure 2 summarizes the repeated procedure used for each temperature trial.
items.explanation: Trial D normally refers to 40 C in Table 1, but the stated error changes its temperature to 30 C. The 30 C curve in Figure 1 ends at 43 units, matching the 30 C entry in Table 1.

items.tests: Predicting the result of a trial that was not run, from the pattern that was.

items.stem: Why did the procedure in Figure 2 place the product measurement after the incubation step, rather than immediately after mixing, and how is this supported by Figure 1?
choices: Measurement after incubation keeps enzyme volume constant, whereas enzyme volume changes with temperature in Table 1.
Measurement after incubation identifies the highest temperature, whereas the curves all have identical endpoints.
Incubation prevents the enzyme and substrate from being mixed, whereas the curves begin above 0 units.
Incubation allows product to accumulate, whereas the curves begin at 0 units immediately after mixing.
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how incubation temperature affected an enzyme that converts a substrate into a colored product. In each trial, the same amounts of enzyme and substrate were mixed, incubated at a selected temperature, and sampled over time. Table 1 lists the trial temperatures and the product measured after 8 minutes, while Figure 1 shows product accumulation during the incubation. Figure 2 summarizes the repeated procedure used for each temperature trial.
items.explanation: Figure 2 shows that measurement follows incubation, and Figure 1 shows product increasing from 0 as time passes. Thus incubation provides time for product to accumulate before measurement.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 shows that measurement follows incubation, and Figure 1 shows product increasing from 0 as time passes. Thus incubation provides time for product to accumulate before measurement.
per_choice.trap: The third choice reverses the procedure and misreads the starting values; the third confuses a controlled amount with the timing of measurement; the fourth contradicts the different endpoints.

items.stem: A follow-up trial uses half as much substrate as the trials in Table 1. If product formation is directly proportional to substrate amount under these conditions, what product amount should be expected at 20 C after 8 minutes, using Table 1 and the stated relationship?
choices: 10.5 units
14.5 units
29 units
43 units
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how incubation temperature affected an enzyme that converts a substrate into a colored product. In each trial, the same amounts of enzyme and substrate were mixed, incubated at a selected temperature, and sampled over time. Table 1 lists the trial temperatures and the product measured after 8 minutes, while Figure 1 shows product accumulation during the incubation. Figure 2 summarizes the repeated procedure used for each temperature trial.
items.explanation: The 20 C trial produced 29 units with the standard substrate amount. Half the substrate gives half the product: 29 ÷ 2 = 14.5 units.

per_choice.correct: The 20 C trial produced 29 units with the standard substrate amount. Half the substrate gives half the product: 29 ÷ 2 = 14.5 units.
per_choice.trap: 29 ignores the changed substrate amount, 43 uses the 30 C row, and 10.5 does not equal half of the correct 20 C value.

items.stem: Which hypothesis best reconciles the early portions of Figure 1 with the 8-minute results in Table 1?
choices: At 30 C, production begins faster, but at 40 C it continues increasing more strongly through 8 minutes.
At 30 C and 40 C, production is identical throughout incubation, but Table 1 uses different enzyme amounts.
At 40 C, production begins faster and remains higher at every measured time than at 30 C.
At 50 C, production begins fastest, but the temperature prevents any product from accumulating after 2 minutes.
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how incubation temperature affected an enzyme that converts a substrate into a colored product. In each trial, the same amounts of enzyme and substrate were mixed, incubated at a selected temperature, and sampled over time. Table 1 lists the trial temperatures and the product measured after 8 minutes, while Figure 1 shows product accumulation during the incubation. Figure 2 summarizes the repeated procedure used for each temperature trial.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows 30 C at 16 units versus 15 units for 40 C at 2 minutes, so 30 C begins slightly faster. By 8 minutes, Table 1 and Figure 1 show 40 C at 51 units versus 43 units at 30 C, so 40 C has the stronger later increase.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows 30 C at 16 units versus 15 units for 40 C at 2 minutes, so 30 C begins slightly faster. By 8 minutes, Table 1 and Figure 1 show 40 C at 51 units versus 43 units at 30 C, so 40 C has the stronger later increase.
per_choice.trap: The third choice overlooks the early crossing of the 30 C and 40 C curves; the third contradicts both displays and the equal enzyme amounts; the fourth misreads the 50 C curve.

items.stem: To make the unrun 35 C trial a valid comparison with the existing trials, which procedure would be required according to Figure 2 and the controls shown in Table 1?
choices: Use the same substrate amount but change enzyme volume to 1.0 mL so the new trial has a midpoint result.
Use 2.0 mL enzyme but double the substrate amount and shorten incubation to 4 minutes at 35 C.
Use 2.0 mL enzyme and the same substrate amount and 8-minute incubation, changing only the temperature to 35 C.
Use the 40 C temperature during incubation and record the product at 35 minutes.
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how incubation temperature affected an enzyme that converts a substrate into a colored product. In each trial, the same amounts of enzyme and substrate were mixed, incubated at a selected temperature, and sampled over time. Table 1 lists the trial temperatures and the product measured after 8 minutes, while Figure 1 shows product accumulation during the incubation. Figure 2 summarizes the repeated procedure used for each temperature trial.
items.explanation: Figure 2 indicates that temperature is set before incubation and product is measured afterward. Table 1 shows that enzyme volume and the 8-minute measurement condition are held constant, so only temperature should change to 35 C.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 indicates that temperature is set before incubation and product is measured afterward. Table 1 shows that enzyme volume and the 8-minute measurement condition are held constant, so only temperature should change to 35 C.
per_choice.trap: The other choices change substrate, enzyme amount, incubation temperature, or measurement time, so their results could not be attributed solely to the new temperature.

items.stem: At 4 klux, what was the ratio of the increase in O2 concentration to the decrease in CO2 concentration? Use Table 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers placed equal amounts of an aquatic plant in sealed chambers and exposed the chambers to different light intensities for 90 min. Dissolved carbon dioxide and oxygen concentrations were measured before and after each trial. Table 1 shows the measurements for each light intensity, Figure 1 relates final carbon dioxide concentration to the change in oxygen concentration, and Figure 2 represents the carbon-exchange process occurring in the plant. In this process, photosynthesis uses dissolved carbon dioxide and produces oxygen, whereas respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
items.explanation: At 4 klux, O2 increased by 8.4 - 6.0 = 2.4 mg/L, while CO2 decreased by 8.0 - 5.0 = 3.0 mg/L. The ratio is 2.4/3.0 = 0.80.

per_choice.correct: At 4 klux, O2 increased by 8.4 - 6.0 = 2.4 mg/L, while CO2 decreased by 8.0 - 5.0 = 3.0 mg/L. The ratio is 2.4/3.0 = 0.80.

items.stem: Compared with the 0-klux trial, how much greater was the net change in O2 concentration in the 6-klux trial? Use Table 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers placed equal amounts of an aquatic plant in sealed chambers and exposed the chambers to different light intensities for 90 min. Dissolved carbon dioxide and oxygen concentrations were measured before and after each trial. Table 1 shows the measurements for each light intensity, Figure 1 relates final carbon dioxide concentration to the change in oxygen concentration, and Figure 2 represents the carbon-exchange process occurring in the plant. In this process, photosynthesis uses dissolved carbon dioxide and produces oxygen, whereas respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
items.explanation: At 0 klux, O2 changed by 5.1 - 6.0 = -0.9 mg/L. At 6 klux, it changed by 9.6 - 6.0 = 3.6 mg/L. The difference is 3.6 - (-0.9) = 4.5 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: At 0 klux, O2 changed by 5.1 - 6.0 = -0.9 mg/L. At 6 klux, it changed by 9.6 - 6.0 = 3.6 mg/L. The difference is 3.6 - (-0.9) = 4.5 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: 3.60 mg/L is the change in the 6-klux chamber alone; 0.90 mg/L is the magnitude of the dark-trial decrease.

items.stem: What was the average rate of CO2 change during the 2-klux trial, expressed per 30 min? Use Table 1.
choices: -1.50 mg/L per 30 min
-0.50 mg/L per 30 min
0.50 mg/L per 30 min
1.50 mg/L per 30 min
items.stimulus: Researchers placed equal amounts of an aquatic plant in sealed chambers and exposed the chambers to different light intensities for 90 min. Dissolved carbon dioxide and oxygen concentrations were measured before and after each trial. Table 1 shows the measurements for each light intensity, Figure 1 relates final carbon dioxide concentration to the change in oxygen concentration, and Figure 2 represents the carbon-exchange process occurring in the plant. In this process, photosynthesis uses dissolved carbon dioxide and produces oxygen, whereas respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
items.explanation: CO2 changed from 8.0 to 6.5 mg/L, a change of -1.5 mg/L over 90 min. Since 90 min contains three 30-min intervals, the rate was -1.5/3 = -0.50 mg/L per 30 min.

per_choice.correct: CO2 changed from 8.0 to 6.5 mg/L, a change of -1.5 mg/L over 90 min. Since 90 min contains three 30-min intervals, the rate was -1.5/3 = -0.50 mg/L per 30 min.
per_choice.trap: The value -1.50 is the total change, not the change per 30 min; positive values reverse the direction of the change.

items.tests: A difference, ratio, rate or average computed from displayed values.

items.stem: Between final CO2 concentrations of 5.0 mg/L and 8.0 mg/L, what was the average change in O2 concentration per 1 mg/L increase in final CO2? Use Figure 1.
choices: -1.20 mg/L O2 per mg/L CO2
-0.80 mg/L O2 per mg/L CO2
-0.40 mg/L O2 per mg/L CO2
0.80 mg/L O2 per mg/L CO2
items.stimulus: Researchers placed equal amounts of an aquatic plant in sealed chambers and exposed the chambers to different light intensities for 90 min. Dissolved carbon dioxide and oxygen concentrations were measured before and after each trial. Table 1 shows the measurements for each light intensity, Figure 1 relates final carbon dioxide concentration to the change in oxygen concentration, and Figure 2 represents the carbon-exchange process occurring in the plant. In this process, photosynthesis uses dissolved carbon dioxide and produces oxygen, whereas respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows O2 changes of 2.4 mg/L at 5.0 mg/L CO2 and 0.0 mg/L at 8.0 mg/L CO2. Thus, the slope is (0.0 - 2.4)/(8.0 - 5.0) = -0.80.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 shows O2 changes of 2.4 mg/L at 5.0 mg/L CO2 and 0.0 mg/L at 8.0 mg/L CO2. Thus, the slope is (0.0 - 2.4)/(8.0 - 5.0) = -0.80.
per_choice.trap: The -1.20 value uses the 5.0-to-6.5 interval; the positive value reverses the downward trend.

items.tests: A difference, ratio, rate or average computed from displayed values.

items.stem: For the 6-klux trial, what was the difference between the change in O2 measured in Table 1 and the change predicted by Figure 1 from its final CO2 concentration? Use Table 1 and Figure 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers placed equal amounts of an aquatic plant in sealed chambers and exposed the chambers to different light intensities for 90 min. Dissolved carbon dioxide and oxygen concentrations were measured before and after each trial. Table 1 shows the measurements for each light intensity, Figure 1 relates final carbon dioxide concentration to the change in oxygen concentration, and Figure 2 represents the carbon-exchange process occurring in the plant. In this process, photosynthesis uses dissolved carbon dioxide and produces oxygen, whereas respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
items.explanation: The 6-klux trial ended at 3.5 mg/L CO2. Figure 1 gives an O2 change of 3.6 mg/L at that CO2 concentration, and Table 1 gives 9.6 - 6.0 = 3.6 mg/L. Their difference is 0.00 mg/L.

per_choice.trap: 3.60 mg/L is the shared change, not the difference between the two displays; 0.60 comes from comparing the final O2 concentration with its initial value incorrectly.

items.tests: A difference, ratio, rate or average computed from displayed values.

items.stem: Define photosynthetic efficiency as the increase in O2 divided by the decrease in CO2. What was the ratio of this efficiency at 2 klux to that at 4 klux? Use Table 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers placed equal amounts of an aquatic plant in sealed chambers and exposed the chambers to different light intensities for 90 min. Dissolved carbon dioxide and oxygen concentrations were measured before and after each trial. Table 1 shows the measurements for each light intensity, Figure 1 relates final carbon dioxide concentration to the change in oxygen concentration, and Figure 2 represents the carbon-exchange process occurring in the plant. In this process, photosynthesis uses dissolved carbon dioxide and produces oxygen, whereas respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

per_choice.trap: 0.80 is the efficiency at either trial, not the ratio of the two efficiencies; 1.60 combines the two efficiencies instead of dividing them.

items.stem: A fifth chamber ended with a final CO2 concentration of 6.0 mg/L. Assuming the relationship in Figure 1 is linear between the neighboring plotted points, what change in O2 concentration would be expected? Use Figure 1 and Figure 2.
items.stimulus: Researchers placed equal amounts of an aquatic plant in sealed chambers and exposed the chambers to different light intensities for 90 min. Dissolved carbon dioxide and oxygen concentrations were measured before and after each trial. Table 1 shows the measurements for each light intensity, Figure 1 relates final carbon dioxide concentration to the change in oxygen concentration, and Figure 2 represents the carbon-exchange process occurring in the plant. In this process, photosynthesis uses dissolved carbon dioxide and produces oxygen, whereas respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
items.explanation: At 5.0 mg/L CO2, the O2 change is 2.4 mg/L; at 6.5 mg/L CO2, it is 1.2 mg/L. A concentration of 6.0 mg/L is 1.0 of the 1.5 mg/L interval, or two-thirds of the way across, so the O2 change is 2.4 - (2/3)(1.2) = 1.6 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: At 5.0 mg/L CO2, the O2 change is 2.4 mg/L; at 6.5 mg/L CO2, it is 1.2 mg/L. A concentration of 6.0 mg/L is 1.0 of the 1.5 mg/L interval, or two-thirds of the way across, so the O2 change is 2.4 - (2/3)(1.2) = 1.6 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: 1.20 and 2.40 are the endpoint values; 2.00 results from treating 6.0 mg/L as halfway between 5.0 and 6.5.

items.stem: A researcher concludes that the low chlorophyll concentration at 7 m was caused by phosphate limitation. Which evaluation is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: The conclusion is not supported because all three samples had identical oxygen changes during the bottle trial.
The conclusion is supported because phosphate and chlorophyll were measured at the same depths.
The conclusion is not supported by phosphate data because phosphate increased as chlorophyll decreased; Figure 1 also does not establish causation.
The conclusion is supported because the 7 m sample had the lowest dissolved-oxygen concentration.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated whether differences in pond depth could explain changes in phytoplankton abundance and dissolved oxygen. Water was collected at 1 m, 3 m, and 7 m and placed in sealed bottles kept in the dark for 24 hours. Table 1 shows phosphate concentration and chlorophyll concentration at each sampling depth, Figure 1 shows dissolved oxygen in the bottles over time, and Figure 2 shows the pond layers and the locations of the samples. Because the bottles were kept in the dark, photosynthesis could not occur during the bottle measurements.

items.stem: Which interpretation of the chlorophyll and oxygen results is most defensible when Table 1, Figure 1, and the bottle condition described in the passage are considered together?
choices: The deep sample had less chlorophyll because darkness caused its phytoplankton to photosynthesize less than the shallow sample.
The shallow sample had more chlorophyll and nearly stable oxygen in darkness, which is consistent with an association but does not prove that chlorophyll caused the oxygen pattern.
The deeper samples had less chlorophyll, and their oxygen declined more, proving that chlorophyll directly consumed oxygen.
The oxygen decline at 7 m proves that the high phosphate concentration there was used by phytoplankton.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated whether differences in pond depth could explain changes in phytoplankton abundance and dissolved oxygen. Water was collected at 1 m, 3 m, and 7 m and placed in sealed bottles kept in the dark for 24 hours. Table 1 shows phosphate concentration and chlorophyll concentration at each sampling depth, Figure 1 shows dissolved oxygen in the bottles over time, and Figure 2 shows the pond layers and the locations of the samples. Because the bottles were kept in the dark, photosynthesis could not occur during the bottle measurements.
items.explanation: Table 1 gives the chlorophyll pattern and Figure 1 gives the oxygen pattern, but the dark bottles remove photosynthesis and the observational depth comparison does not isolate chlorophyll as a cause. Thus the results show an association, not proof of direct causation.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 gives the chlorophyll pattern and Figure 1 gives the oxygen pattern, but the dark bottles remove photosynthesis and the observational depth comparison does not isolate chlorophyll as a cause. Thus the results show an association, not proof of direct causation.
per_choice.trap: The third choice overstates a correlation, the third incorrectly says photosynthesis occurred in darkness, and the fourth treats oxygen loss as evidence of phosphate use.

items.stem: The researchers want to test whether low oxygen, rather than depth itself, causes low chlorophyll concentration. Which additional procedure would best address that question using the patterns in Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: Divide water collected at one depth into groups with different controlled oxygen concentrations while holding phosphate, light, and temperature constant.
Add phosphate to the 7 m water and compare its chlorophyll with the untreated 1 m water.
Measure dissolved oxygen at 3 m for a longer time but do not measure chlorophyll again.
Compare the existing 1 m and 7 m samples again, without changing their oxygen concentrations.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated whether differences in pond depth could explain changes in phytoplankton abundance and dissolved oxygen. Water was collected at 1 m, 3 m, and 7 m and placed in sealed bottles kept in the dark for 24 hours. Table 1 shows phosphate concentration and chlorophyll concentration at each sampling depth, Figure 1 shows dissolved oxygen in the bottles over time, and Figure 2 shows the pond layers and the locations of the samples. Because the bottles were kept in the dark, photosynthesis could not occur during the bottle measurements.
items.explanation: The existing samples differ in depth, phosphate, chlorophyll, and initial oxygen, so they cannot isolate oxygen. Manipulating oxygen within water from the same depth while controlling other factors would directly test its effect on chlorophyll.

per_choice.correct: The existing samples differ in depth, phosphate, chlorophyll, and initial oxygen, so they cannot isolate oxygen. Manipulating oxygen within water from the same depth while controlling other factors would directly test its effect on chlorophyll.
per_choice.trap: The first and second choices retain multiple confounding differences, and the fourth measures oxygen without testing the proposed response variable.

items.stem: Which evaluation of the stated bacterial-conversion model is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: The model is untested because only the final NH3 concentration, not any intermediate concentration, was measured.
The model is supported solely because the discharge NH3 concentration is lower than the intake concentration.
The model is contradicted because NO3− does not increase until after the biofilter.
The model is supported: at the biofilter, NH3 decreases while NO3− increases under oxygen-rich conditions, although the data alone do not prove that bacteria caused the change.
items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: At the transition into and through the biofilter, NH3 falls from 16 to 7 mg/L while NO3− rises from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L; Table 1 also shows 6.4 mg/L DO there. This supports the predicted pattern but does not by itself establish bacterial causation.

per_choice.correct: At the transition into and through the biofilter, NH3 falls from 16 to 7 mg/L while NO3− rises from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L; Table 1 also shows 6.4 mg/L DO there. This supports the predicted pattern but does not by itself establish bacterial causation.
per_choice.trap: The last choice uses the correct overall decrease but ignores where the decrease and nitrate increase occur; the third choice mistakes the small post-biofilter nitrate increase for evidence against conversion in the biofilter.

items.stem: What percentage of the intake NH3 concentration has been removed by the time the water reaches the biofilter stage? Use Table 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: NH3 decreases from 18 mg/L at intake to 7 mg/L at the biofilter, so the decrease is 11 mg/L. The percentage removed is 11/18 × 100 = 61.1%.

per_choice.correct: NH3 decreases from 18 mg/L at intake to 7 mg/L at the biofilter, so the decrease is 11 mg/L. The percentage removed is 11/18 × 100 = 61.1%.
per_choice.trap: 50.0% results from using the biofilter value as the denominator; 66.7% comes from comparing the decrease with the biofilter value rather than the intake value.

items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: From aeration to biofilter, NH3 decreases from 16 to 7 mg/L, a 9 mg/L decrease, while NO3− increases from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L, a 5.4 mg/L increase. Both changes exceed those at the other transitions.

per_choice.correct: From aeration to biofilter, NH3 decreases from 16 to 7 mg/L, a 9 mg/L decrease, while NO3− increases from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L, a 5.4 mg/L increase. Both changes exceed those at the other transitions.
per_choice.trap: The intake-to-aeration transition has the largest DO increase, but DO is not the requested quantity; the later transitions can look important because NO3− is already high there.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which comparison would best test whether the biofilter, rather than merely the passage of time through the treatment system, is responsible for the major NH3-to-NO3− change?
choices: Increase aeration while leaving the biofilter in place and compare the resulting discharge with the original intake.
Measure the same discharge sample twice to determine whether its NH3 concentration is stable.
Compare intake water with discharge water, without changing the treatment path.
Route a comparable stream through aeration and settling but bypass the biofilter, then measure NH3 and NO3− at discharge.
items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: A stream that follows the same general path but bypasses the biofilter isolates the presence of the biofilter as the key difference. Measuring both NH3 and NO3− tests the predicted conversion rather than only total removal.

per_choice.correct: A stream that follows the same general path but bypasses the biofilter isolates the presence of the biofilter as the key difference. Measuring both NH3 and NO3− tests the predicted conversion rather than only total removal.
per_choice.trap: The first and second choices provide no biofilter comparison, while the third changes aeration and therefore introduces another possible cause of any change.

items.stem: According to Figure 1, during which adjacent interval does the reaction rate first change from increasing to decreasing?
choices: pH 6 to pH 7
pH 7 to pH 8
pH 4 to pH 5
pH 8 to pH 9
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how pH affected the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction. Equal amounts of enzyme and hydrogen peroxide were mixed in buffered solutions, and oxygen production was measured after 60 s; reaction rate was calculated as oxygen volume divided by 60 s. Table 1 shows raw oxygen volumes for selected pH values, Figure 1 shows mean reaction rates across a wider pH range, and Figure 2 shows where the tested pH values fall on the pH scale. All other experimental conditions were held constant.
items.explanation: The plotted rate rises through pH 7, then falls from 0.40 mL/min at pH 7 to 0.37 mL/min at pH 8.

per_choice.correct: The plotted rate rises through pH 7, then falls from 0.40 mL/min at pH 7 to 0.37 mL/min at pH 8.
per_choice.trap: Choosing pH 6 to pH 7 confuses the last increasing interval with the first decreasing interval.

items.tests: Whether a quantity rises, falls, or turns, and over which interval.

items.stem: The first point in Figure 1 at which dissolved oxygen is exactly 8.0 mg/L corresponds to which combination of information from Table 1 and Figure 2?
choices: 8 min; Light phase; Photosynthesis follows
8 min; Dark phase; Respiration follows
12 min; Light phase; O2 measurement follows
12 min; Dark phase; Dark exposure follows
items.stimulus: A student measured dissolved oxygen in an algae-containing microcosm during a repeating light-dark process. Oxygen concentration was recorded every 4 minutes while the microcosm was illuminated from 0 to 12 minutes and kept dark from 12 to 24 minutes. Table 1 lists the measurements and the lighting phase, while Figure 1 graphs the same measurements against time. Figure 2 represents the sequence of exposure, biological activity, and oxygen measurement used in each cycle.
items.explanation: Figure 1 first reaches 8.0 mg/L at 8 minutes. Table 1 identifies that time as Light, and in Figure 2 light exposure leads to photosynthesis.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 first reaches 8.0 mg/L at 8 minutes. Table 1 identifies that time as Light, and in Figure 2 light exposure leads to photosynthesis.
per_choice.trap: The 12-minute row is the maximum-oxygen row, not the first row at 8.0 mg/L; the dark-phase rows begin after 12 minutes.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, what was the average rate of dissolved-oxygen increase from 4 to 12 minutes?
choices: 0.19 mg/L/min
0.38 mg/L/min
0.50 mg/L/min
1.50 mg/L/min
items.stimulus: A student measured dissolved oxygen in an algae-containing microcosm during a repeating light-dark process. Oxygen concentration was recorded every 4 minutes while the microcosm was illuminated from 0 to 12 minutes and kept dark from 12 to 24 minutes. Table 1 lists the measurements and the lighting phase, while Figure 1 graphs the same measurements against time. Figure 2 represents the sequence of exposure, biological activity, and oxygen measurement used in each cycle.
items.explanation: The concentration increased from 7.1 to 8.6 mg/L, a change of 1.5 mg/L over 8 minutes. The average rate was 1.5 ÷ 8 = 0.1875, or about 0.19 mg/L/min.

16-20 min; Dark
20-24 min; Dark
8-12 min; Light
items.stimulus: A student measured dissolved oxygen in an algae-containing microcosm during a repeating light-dark process. Oxygen concentration was recorded every 4 minutes while the microcosm was illuminated from 0 to 12 minutes and kept dark from 12 to 24 minutes. Table 1 lists the measurements and the lighting phase, while Figure 1 graphs the same measurements against time. Figure 2 represents the sequence of exposure, biological activity, and oxygen measurement used in each cycle.
items.explanation: The changes over the three downward intervals are -0.5, -0.6, and -0.5 mg/L, each over 4 minutes. Therefore 16-20 minutes has the steepest decline, and Table 1 labels it Dark.

items.tests: Recognising which graph represents a given table, or the reverse.

items.stem: If the straight-line trend between 4 and 8 minutes in Figure 1 is extended only to 6 minutes, what dissolved-oxygen value should be estimated from Table 1?
items.stimulus: A student measured dissolved oxygen in an algae-containing microcosm during a repeating light-dark process. Oxygen concentration was recorded every 4 minutes while the microcosm was illuminated from 0 to 12 minutes and kept dark from 12 to 24 minutes. Table 1 lists the measurements and the lighting phase, while Figure 1 graphs the same measurements against time. Figure 2 represents the sequence of exposure, biological activity, and oxygen measurement used in each cycle.
items.explanation: The values at 4 and 8 minutes are 7.1 and 8.0 mg/L. Six minutes is halfway between them, so the estimate is 7.1 + (0.9 ÷ 2) = 7.55 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: The values at 4 and 8 minutes are 7.1 and 8.0 mg/L. Six minutes is halfway between them, so the estimate is 7.1 + (0.9 ÷ 2) = 7.55 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: 7.75 treats 6 minutes as halfway from 7.5 rather than from the actual 4-minute value; 8.05 uses the later endpoint and overshoots the segment.

items.tests: Recognising which graph represents a given table, or the reverse.

items.stem: What is the ratio of the magnitude of the oxygen increase during the light phase to the magnitude of the oxygen decrease during the dark phase, using Table 1 and the direction shown in Figure 1?
items.stimulus: A student measured dissolved oxygen in an algae-containing microcosm during a repeating light-dark process. Oxygen concentration was recorded every 4 minutes while the microcosm was illuminated from 0 to 12 minutes and kept dark from 12 to 24 minutes. Table 1 lists the measurements and the lighting phase, while Figure 1 graphs the same measurements against time. Figure 2 represents the sequence of exposure, biological activity, and oxygen measurement used in each cycle.
items.explanation: During light, oxygen changes from 6.2 to 8.6 mg/L, an increase of 2.4 mg/L. During dark, it changes from 8.6 to 7.0 mg/L, a decrease of 1.6 mg/L. The ratio is 2.4 ÷ 1.6 = 1.50.

per_choice.correct: During light, oxygen changes from 6.2 to 8.6 mg/L, an increase of 2.4 mg/L. During dark, it changes from 8.6 to 7.0 mg/L, a decrease of 1.6 mg/L. The ratio is 2.4 ÷ 1.6 = 1.50.
per_choice.trap: 0.67 reverses the requested ratio; 2.40 reports the light-phase change without comparing it with the dark-phase change.

items.tests: Recognising which graph represents a given table, or the reverse.

items.stem: The student hypothesizes that the decline after 12 minutes is associated with the dark-exposure and respiration stages in Figure 2. Which observation from Table 1 and Figure 1 most directly supports that hypothesis rather than merely showing that oxygen declined?
choices: The largest oxygen value was 8.6 mg/L at 12 minutes, when the phase changed
Oxygen increased during the Light rows and decreased in every Dark row after the O2 measurement at 12 minutes
The oxygen value at 24 minutes was 7.0 mg/L, which was lower than the value at 0 minutes
Oxygen was 8.0 mg/L at 8 minutes, which occurred before the maximum value
items.stimulus: A student measured dissolved oxygen in an algae-containing microcosm during a repeating light-dark process. Oxygen concentration was recorded every 4 minutes while the microcosm was illuminated from 0 to 12 minutes and kept dark from 12 to 24 minutes. Table 1 lists the measurements and the lighting phase, while Figure 1 graphs the same measurements against time. Figure 2 represents the sequence of exposure, biological activity, and oxygen measurement used in each cycle.
items.explanation: The hypothesis links the direction of change to the phases in the cycle. The complete pattern—rise through the light rows followed by a decline across all dark rows—matches that phase-based prediction.

per_choice.correct: The hypothesis links the direction of change to the phases in the cycle. The complete pattern—rise through the light rows followed by a decline across all dark rows—matches that phase-based prediction.
per_choice.trap: The other choices identify individual values or comparisons but do not connect the trend to the light and dark stages.

items.stem: To test whether the downward portion of Figure 1 is caused specifically by darkness rather than by elapsed time or repeated measurement, which modification would provide the strongest comparison while preserving the cycle in Figure 2?
choices: Repeat the original cycle without recording the oxygen concentration at 12 minutes
Run a second microcosm in darkness for 24 minutes, but measure oxygen only at 12 and 24 minutes
Repeat the original cycle with a different algae volume but use the same light and dark schedule
Run a second microcosm for 24 minutes with light maintained after 12 minutes, measuring oxygen at the same times
items.stimulus: A student measured dissolved oxygen in an algae-containing microcosm during a repeating light-dark process. Oxygen concentration was recorded every 4 minutes while the microcosm was illuminated from 0 to 12 minutes and kept dark from 12 to 24 minutes. Table 1 lists the measurements and the lighting phase, while Figure 1 graphs the same measurements against time. Figure 2 represents the sequence of exposure, biological activity, and oxygen measurement used in each cycle.
items.explanation: Keeping all timing and measurements the same while replacing the dark exposure with continued light isolates darkness as the changed factor. A comparison of the post-12-minute trends can then test whether the decline depends on darkness.

per_choice.correct: Keeping all timing and measurements the same while replacing the dark exposure with continued light isolates darkness as the changed factor. A comparison of the post-12-minute trends can then test whether the decline depends on darkness.
per_choice.trap: The all-dark condition changes the light history and has too few measurements; changing algae volume adds a new variable, and omitting a measurement removes the key transition point.

items.stem: Using the model stated in the passage and the units for L and T shown in Figure 1, what period would the model predict for a pendulum with L = 1.44 m, beyond the lengths tested in Table 1?
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how the length of a pendulum affects its period, the time for one complete swing back to its starting position. For each length, they used the apparatus shown in Figure 2 and measured two periods, then calculated the mean. Table 1 lists the individual measurements and means, while Figure 1 plots the means against pendulum length. The model for an ideal pendulum is T = 2π√(L/g), which is approximately T = 2√L when L is in meters and g is 9.8 m/s². The model is intended to predict periods for lengths beyond those tested.

per_choice.trap: A value of 2.20 s comes from treating the period as proportional to L rather than to √L; larger choices overextend the measured trend.
